papers.title: Pathways to Protection: Factors Associated With Decreased Mental Health and Suicide Risk in US High School Students by Gender and Sexual Identity.
papers.abstract: Depression and suicidality among US youth have increased over the past decades, with disproportionately high rates found for youth who are lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, or questioning (LGBTQ+). Prior research has identified protective factors that predict lower rates of depressive symptoms and suicide risk among all youth. However, less is known about whether these factors are equally protective across subpopulations. We examined the prevalence of protective factors by sex at birth and sexual/gender identity and how associations with mental health outcomes vary by group. This study analyzes data from the 2023 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, a cross-sectional survey conducted with high school students by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. We build on previous Centers for Disease Control and Prevention analyses by examining the same set of mental health and suicide risk indicators and protective factors by sex at birth (male vs. female), sexual/gender identity (cisgender-heterosexual vs. LGBTQ+), and the combination thereof. Rates of protective factors varied by subgroup. Not all factors were equally protective across sex and sexual/gender identity, and different factors appeared relevant for different outcomes. Across logistic regression models, having basic needs met, school connectedness, and sleep emerged as more consistently related to mental health and suicide risk than other factors. Both the prevalence and significance of protective factors varied by sex at birth and sexual/gender identity, suggesting that not all factors are equally protective for vulnerable young people. When designing efforts to support youth mental health, strategies should consider the needs of different subgroups to ensure that all youth are benefitting from supportive practices.
papers.journal: The Journal of adolescent health : official publication of the Society for Adolescent Medicine

papers.title: Process, Heterogeneity, and Modifiable Risk Factors of Postoperative Recovery After Cardiac Surgery.
papers.abstract: Cardiac surgery improves clinical endpoints but imposes challenges in recovery. Understanding patient-reported postoperative recovery is crucial for optimal care. The goal of this study was to reveal the process, heterogeneity, and modifiable risk factors of patient-reported postoperative recovery. In this multicenter prospective cohort study involving patients undergoing nonemergent cardiac surgery, patient-reported outcomes were assessed using the Fuwai-Cardiac Recovery Scale (a 9-item scale including symptoms and functional status) at baseline and 8 timepoints after surgery (days 1-4, weeks 2 and 3, and months 1 and 3). Total score and each item score of the Fuwai-Cardiac Recovery Scale were reported to characterize the recovery process. Group-based trajectory models were applied to detect heterogeneity, and trajectory with the largest area under trajectory curve was defined as poor recovery pattern. Multivariable stepwise regression was performed to uncover modifiable risk factors of poor recovery. From May 2023 to December 2024, 2,993 patients from 8 Chinese centers were enrolled. The proportions of patients achieving a total score ≤30 (less likely to experience 3-month unplanned readmission) were 77.4% at discharge (week 2) and 97.7% at month 3. Areas under the curve of the item score within 2 weeks, ranked from highest to lowest, were thirst, toileting dependency, poor mobility, fatigue, pain, poor sleep, poor appetite, shortness of breath, and nausea or vomiting. Three different poor recovery patterns were identified: 1) "initial worsening followed by improving" in shortness of breath, poor appetite, nausea or vomiting, poor sleep, and pain; 2) "persistently not improving" in thirst; and 3) "slowly improving" in fatigue, poor mobility, and toileting dependency. Several modifiable risk factors were significantly associated with poor recovery patterns, including smoking (shortness of breath, OR: 1.55; 95% CI: 1.07-2.24), obesity (poor mobility, OR: 1.52; 95% CI: 1.02-2.26), and anemia (poor appetite, OR: 1.47; 95% CI: 1.11-1.95; fatigue, OR: 1.36; 95% CI: 1.11-1.67). Recovery after cardiac surgery is a dynamic trajectory that unfolds over time, differs substantially among patients, and offers opportunities for earlier recognition and intervention.
papers.journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology

papers.title: Compassion Fatigue in General and Psychiatric Hospital Nurses: A Systematic Review of Patterns, Determinants, and Consequences.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Compassion fatigue (CF), commonly discussed alongside burnout and secondary traumatic stress, is an important occupational concern in nursing. General and psychiatric hospital environments expose nurses to different combinations of organizational, emotional, and relational demands. This systematic review aimed to synthesize and compare the reported patterns, determinants, and consequences of compassion fatigue among nurses working in general and psychiatric hospital settings and to identify setting-specific factors relevant to nursing practice and workforce support. Methods: The review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020. PubMed, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and Scopus were searched for peer-reviewed studies published from 2020 to 2025. Quantitative and qualitative hospital-based nursing studies reporting CF or closely related professional-quality-of-life constructs were eligible. Methodological quality was appraised using Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tools, and findings were synthesized narratively because of heterogeneity in study designs, instruments, and reporting formats. Results: Eighteen studies were included after screening 302 records identified in the database searches. Moderate-to-high CF-related burden was reported across both general and psychiatric settings, but direct prevalence comparisons were not appropriate because instruments, definitions, and thresholds differed substantially. General-hospital studies more often emphasized workload, high acuity, staffing pressures, sleep disruption, and acute trauma exposure, whereas psychiatric studies more often emphasized moral distress, aggression or workplace violence, stigma, and prolonged emotionally demanding therapeutic relationships. Across settings, CF was associated with poorer psychological and occupational well-being. Conclusions: The available evidence supports setting-sensitive prevention and workforce-support strategies but does not establish that one hospital setting has a uniformly higher prevalence of CF. More consistent definitions, measurement tools, and reporting thresholds are needed to enable reliable cross-setting comparisons.

papers.title: Digital Fatigue, Workforce Readiness, and Medication Safety: A Systems Perspective for Pharmacy Education.
papers.abstract: The increasing integration of digital technologies into pharmacy education has transformed how students learn, communicate, and develop professional competencies. However, prolonged engagement with digital platforms may contribute to digital fatigue, technostress, cognitive overload, sleep disruption, and reduced well-being. Although digital fatigue has primarily been considered a learner wellness concern, its potential implications may extend to workforce readiness and medication safety. Cognitive functions affected by fatigue and information overload, including attention, vigilance, working memory, information synthesis, and clinical judgment, are also essential for safe medication use and effective pharmacy practice. This commentary applies a systems and human factors perspective to examine digital fatigue as an emerging consideration in pharmacy education and workforce development. Using principles aligned with the Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety (SEIPS) framework, we highlight potential pathways through which digitally intensive learning environments may influence cognitive performance and preparedness for technology-enabled pharmacy practice. Systems-based strategies are proposed, including intentional digital curriculum design, digital well-being and resilience training, human-centered technology design, sleep and fatigue prevention, and simulation focused on cognitive load management. As pharmacy education continues to evolve alongside technological innovation, greater attention to digital well-being may help prepare pharmacists to practice safely, effectively, and sustainably within increasingly technology-intensive healthcare environments.

papers.title: Combining Peripheral Inflammatory Biomarkers and aEEG Background Monitoring to Predict Neurological Outcome in Neonates Undergoing Cardiac Surgery for Congenital Heart Disease: A Real-World Pilot Experience.
papers.abstract: Background: Neonates with congenital heart disease (CHD) are at increased risk of neurological deficits. We investigated perioperative trajectories of neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) and monocyte-to-albumin ratio (MAR), their association with amplitude-integrated EEG (aEEG) background, and their contribution to short-term neurological outcome prediction. Methods: We retrospectively studied 64 neonates with CHD admitted for surgical evaluation. Combined conventional EEG/amplitude EEG (cEEG/aEEG) monitoring was performed pre-operatively (T0), within 24 h after surgery (T1), and 7-10 days post-operatively (T2). aEEG background was dichotomized as normal or abnormal. NLR and MAR were calculated from routine laboratory parameters. Associations with aEEG background and neurological outcome at intensive care unit discharge were assessed using non-parametric analyses and receiver operating characteristic curves. Results: Both NLR and MAR values showed significant perioperative longitudinal variation, characterized by a transient post-operative increase followed by normalization at one week. NLR demonstrated a consistent association with worsening aEEG background across all timepoints (T0: ρ = 0.566, pFDR < 0.001; ρ = 0.363, pFDR = 0.013; T2: ρ = 0.477, pFDR < 0.001), whereas MAR showed no significant association with neurophysiological abnormalities. Higher T2 NLR was associated with unfavorable short-term neurological outcome (ρ = 0.397, p_FDR = 0.016). T2 aEEG background and NLR showed comparable discriminative performance (AUC = 0.783 and 0.760, respectively). The combined NLR + aEEG model yielded a numerically higher AUC (0.844), although the improvement was not statistically significant. Conclusions: Our findings suggest an exploratory association between perioperative systemic inflammation and neurophysiological dysfunction in neonates with CHD. NLR may represent a potential adjunctive marker of perioperative cerebral dysfunction, although with susceptibility to systemic and perioperative complications. These preliminary findings warrant further investigation of inflammatory biomarkers alongside aEEG monitoring to better characterize their potential role in neurological risk stratification.

papers.title: Tactile Feedback Device Effects on Sensory-Motor Integration in Post-Stroke Finger Impairment: A Single-Case Experimental Multiple-Baseline Study.
papers.abstract: Post-stroke impairment (PSI) frequently causes upper limb sensorimotor deficits, including reduced ability to perceive fingertip friction, limiting dexterous movements. We evaluated the effects of a tactile sensory substitution device ("Yubi-Reco") that delivers real-time fingertip friction information to both temporal bones via vibration and explored potential neurophysiological changes in PSI. This study used a single-case experimental multiple-baseline design. Three participants with PSI completed a 15-day AB-phase protocol. Baseline (A) consisted of daily sensorimotor tasks without Yubi-Reco, while the intervention (B) added real-time friction feedback via Yubi-Reco to the same tasks. Outcomes included electroencephalography (gamma power), the Purdue Pegboard Test, finger numbness Numerical Rating Scale (NRS), Motor Activity Log-14 (Amount of Use [AoU], Quality of Movement [QoM]), and sense of agency (SoA). Effect sizes were calculated using Tau-U. Very large changes were observed in Purdue Pegboard Test performance (Tau-U = 0.80), and large changes were observed in finger numbness NRS scores (Tau-U = 0.79). Case I showed increased gamma power across frontal and central sites, Case II demonstrated relative attenuation near right frontal and parietal sites, and Case III showed bilateral central gamma reduction, suggesting neurophysiological alterations near recorded sites. AoU and SoA improved in all participants. AoU exceeded the minimal clinically important difference (0.5 points) in two cases. Real-time sensory substitution feedback using Yubi-Reco may improve upper-limb sensorimotor function and induce preliminary neurophysiological changes in individuals with PSI. The intervention appeared to enhance dexterous movement ability and SoA, which coincided with preliminary, exploratory neurophysiological shifts across sensorimotor networks.

papers.title: From Mechanistic Insights to Rational Interventions in Parkinson's Disease: An Integrated Approach with a Patient Perspective.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the selective loss of nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons, accompanied by the accumulation and spreading of misfolded α-synuclein aggregates. Proposed mechanisms relevant to PD include gut-brain propagation of pathology via autonomic circuits, autophagy-related maintenance of proteostasis, and sleep-associated glymphatic clearance of extracellular waste. These mechanisms have prompted interest in multimodal approaches targeting disease-relevant biological pathways. Whether such approaches modify the neurodegenerative process or predominantly promote functional adaptation and compensation remains an open question. Methods: In a real-world clinical setting, a single patient with early-stage PD was observed over two years while five interventions targeting disease-relevant pathways were introduced at different time points and partly overlapped. Evaluation included physician-based clinical assessments and patient-reported observations, complemented by wearable-derived monitoring of autonomic and sleep metrics during the final six months. Serial DAT-SPECT imaging at baseline and two-year follow-up assessed changes in DAT binding. Results: Motor impairment remained mild and the patient reported largely stable overall mobility, although the persistent unilateral tremor was perceived to increase gradually later in the observation period. During the final six months, wearable monitoring indicated relative stable nocturnal autonomic measures and no markedly atypical rapid eye movement (REM) sleep estimates, while suggesting reduced slow-wave sleep (SWS). Following implementation of a structured bedtime routine, wearable-derived SWS estimates increased. Serial DAT-SPECT imaging demonstrated lower striatal DAT binding at two-year follow-up despite clinical stability. Conclusions: In this individual case, relative clinical stability coexisted with a longitudinal reduction in striatal DAT binding. Although no inference regarding disease modification can be drawn from a single uncontrolled observation, this discordance illustrates the limitations of interpreting clinical stability alone as evidence of an unchanged underlying disease process.

papers.title: Mapping EEG Microstates Across Physiological States: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Background: Electroencephalographic (EEG) microstates are transient topographic configurations that index large-scale network dynamics at the millisecond scale. Although widely studied clinically, their characterization in healthy subjects remains fragmentary, hindering the separation of normative from pathological dynamics. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020, we searched PubMed, Scopus, Springer, Web of Science and Google Scholar for studies published between June 2019 and June 2025 (PROSPERO CRD420251106374). Of 5052 records, 91 studies were included; risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I. Duration, frequency, coverage, topography and transition probabilities were extracted for classes A-F, and the contributing evidence was characterized by clustering solution size (K = 4 vs. K ≥ 5). Results: Microstates D and C showed the longest mean durations (78.14 and 77.04 ms), A and B intermediate values (69.24 and 66.51 ms) and E and F the shortest (59.93 and 58.75 ms); E and F were supported exclusively by solutions with K ≥ 5. The highest transition probabilities (B ↔ F, E → C) rested on only 4-5 studies, whereas the best-evidenced routes were B → A, B → C, B → D and C → D. Conclusions: These findings are a first step toward a normative reference for healthy adults, contingent on standardizing clustering, filtering and transition metrics.

papers.title: Microcurrent Neuromodulation and Stress-Recovery Markers Across a Competitive Season in Elite Female Soccer Athletes: A Controlled Pilot Study.
papers.abstract: Background: Elite women's soccer involves sustained physical and psychosocial demands that may affect endocrine regulation, autonomic recovery, and sleep across the competitive season. Non-invasive neuromodulation has been proposed as an adjunct recovery strategy; however, longitudinal in-season evidence in elite female athletes remains limited. Methods: This controlled pilot trial included 12 elite female soccer players (mean age of 21.4 ± 5.2 years), allocated in a 1:1 ratio to a NESA intervention group (n = 6) or a no-intervention control group (n = 6). The intervention consisted of 32 sessions delivered over eight weeks, with four sessions per week and no sessions on match days. Outcomes were assessed at five predefined time points across the competitive season. Primary physiological outcomes were salivary cortisol and heart rate variability (HRV), complemented by subjective sleep quality (PSQI), competitive state anxiety (CSAI-2), and menstruation-related quality of life (CVM-22). Results: All participants completed the protocol, and no adverse events were reported. The main finding was observed at the post-intervention assessment (M4), where salivary cortisol concentrations were significantly lower in the NESA group than in the control group (7.62 ± 4.02 vs. 25.90 ± 9.92 µg/dL; independent Student's t-test, t = -4.184, df = 10, p = 0.002). Subjective sleep quality showed divergent descriptive trajectories during the pre-post intervention interval: PSQI scores decreased in the NESA group from M3 to M4 and increased in the control group, although the between-group comparison of change was not statistically significant (p = 0.183). Continuous HRV indices did not show a consistent pattern favouring the NESA group; however, categorical HRV profiles suggested descriptive maintenance of a high HRV classification in the intervention group. No consistent intervention-related effects were observed for competitive state anxiety or menstruation-related quality of life. Conclusions: In this controlled pilot study, an eight-week NESA non-invasive neuromodulation protocol was associated with lower post-intervention salivary cortisol concentrations in elite female soccer players. Sleep and HRV findings should be interpreted as complementary descriptive signals, whereas anxiety and menstruation-related quality of life did not show consistent intervention-related changes. Given the small sample size, open-label design, absence of a sham control, and unadjusted baseline differences in cortisol concentrations and sleep quality between groups, these findings should be considered preliminary and hypothesis-generating. Larger, adequately powered, sham-controlled trials are needed to determine the magnitude, specificity, and practical relevance of these findings.

papers.title: Characterization of Two Functional Assays and Development of Quality Standards Using Tetrodotoxin and µ-Conotoxin KIIIA as Test Compounds Against NaV Channels.
papers.abstract: This study evaluates two commonly used in vitro techniques to assess compound potencies: patch-clamp electrophysiology and fluorescence membrane potential assay. Furthermore, a quality framework to assess Tetrodotoxin and µ-conotoxin KIIIA activity on the voltage-gated sodium (NaV) receptors NaV 1.4 and NaV 1.7 using patch-clamp electrophysiology in a controlled, comparative manner is developed and described. The framework includes verification of cell line receptor overexpression, assay characterization using a well-studied reference compound, data curation, and test compound potency assessment. Data generated here support previous claims that patch-clamp electrophysiology is the gold standard for potency assessments, being a more reproducible and sensitive technique than the fluorescence membrane potential assay. Patch-clamp electrophysiology characterization using nine replicate dose-response curves over three days generated similar half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values to much larger datasets and the existing literature for the sodium channel cell lines selected for these studies. This framework can be adapted by other laboratories for rapid development and characterization of high-throughput, robust, and efficient functional assays to assess quality and consistency of measurements over time.

papers.title: Resting-State Alpha Power and Cross-Hemispheric Beta Connectivity Are Associated With Individual Differences in Voice Identity Perception.
papers.abstract: Human voices convey not only linguistic content but also rich information about speaker identity. Individual differences in voice discrimination are robust and trait-like, yet their neurophysiological substrates remain unclear. In the present study, we investigated whether resting-state electroencephalography (rsEEG) is associated with individual differences in voice identity perception, assessed using the Sisu Voice Matching Test (SVMT). A total of 61 native Mandarin speakers underwent eyes-open and eyes-closed rsEEG recordings, from which spectral power and interchannel coherence were extracted across eight canonical frequency bands. Behavioral performance on SVMT was examined alongside additional cognitive and perceptual measures, and principal component analysis was used to derive orthogonal covariates for specificity analyses, which enabled us to determine whether the rsEEG-SVMT relationships were independent of broader cognitive factors. Our results revealed distinct neural-behavioral associations across resting-state conditions: In eyes-open recordings, alpha-band power was positively associated with accuracy on telling-together trials, while cross-hemispheric beta-band coherence between right frontal and left temporo-parietal regions correlated with overall and pseudo-word performance. In contrast, eyes-closed spectral power showed limited explanatory value, with a specific negative beta coherence between left central and right posterior sites associated with poorer performance. Notably, the alpha power effect was attenuated after controlling for domain-general cognitive factors, whereas the beta coherence-SVMT associations remained robust, indicating greater specificity to voice identity processing. These findings suggest that individual differences in voice discrimination are grounded in stable neural traits that are differentially expressed across background resting-state conditions. Specifically, they support a two-tier framework in which spectral power reflects domain-general cognitive readiness, whereas network-level beta-band connectivity constitutes a more selective neural signature of voice identity perception. https://doi.org/10.23641/asha.34914567.
papers.journal: Journal of speech, language, and hearing research : JSLHR

papers.title: Temporal Structure in Free-Living Wearable Pulse Rate and Pulse Rate Variability: Beyond Daily and Nightly Averages.
papers.abstract: Wearable pulse metrics are typically reported as a single daily, waking, or nightly average. This presentation of the data may mask differences between sleep and wakefulness, temporal variations within a given state, and differences in the amount of signal retained. To determine whether single-value averages provide a representative summary of free-living pulse physiology, we analyzed 28 days of smartwatch and smart-ring data from 35 participants. Sleep and waking periods were identified using the smart-ring sleep data. Pulse rate was obtained from the smartwatch-generated values, and pulse rate variability (PRV) was calculated from the raw photoplethysmography as the root mean square of successive pulse-interval differences (RMSSD) and standard deviation of pulse-to-pulse intervals (SDNN). Analyses compared paired sleep-wake periods and examined temporal variability within both waking and sleep periods. Mean pulse rate was 72.4 beats/min during sleep and 89.1 beats/min during the subsequent waking period (difference: -16.7 beats/min; 95% confidence interval [CI], -23.0 to -10.2). The mean absolute deviation of the five-minute waking pulse-rate measurements from the waking-period mean was 10.89 beats/min (95% CI, 9.75-12.02); on average, 44.6% of waking measurements differed from the mean by more than 10 beats/min. During sleep, the mean absolute deviation from the period mean was 4.30 beats/min (95% CI, 3.17-5.56). From earlier to later sleep, RMSSD increased by 40.8% (95% CI, 18.7-67.5%; q = 0.0001) and SDNN increased by 82.6% (95% CI, 51.4-117.4%; q = 0.0001). Only 8.6% of the waking recordings met the PRV quality criteria, whereas 64.0% of the sleep recordings did. In summary, single-value averages may not capture differences between sleep and wakefulness or temporal structure within states; unequal signal retention may also affect the representativeness of state averages. Therefore, reports of wearable pulse biomarkers should specify sleep-wake state, within-state timing, aggregation method, and signal retention criteria.
papers.journal: Journal of cardiovascular development and disease

papers.title: Inflammatory Biomarkers in Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Meta-Analysis of Circulating Markers and Narrative Synthesis of Local Mediators.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is associated with systemic inflammation, but findings are inconsistent. We compared circulating C-reactive protein (CRP, including high-sensitivity CRP [hs-CRP]), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) in OSA versus non-OSA and narratively synthesized local airway/tonsillar mediators. Following PRISMA 2020 (PROSPERO CRD420261386183), five databases were searched to 10 July 2026. Risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-E/ROBINS-I; standardized mean differences (SMDs) were pooled with restricted maximum likelihood (REML) random-effects models; certainty was graded (GRADE). Of 298 studies, 105 were pooled. OSA was associated with higher CRP/hs-CRP (SMD 0.68, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.48 to 0.88; k = 65), TNF-α (1.41, 0.82 to 1.99; k = 47), and IL-6 (0.94, 0.64 to 1.23; k = 45); IL-1β did not differ significantly (0.64, -0.40 to 1.68; k = 11). Heterogeneity was very high (I2 89.4-97.7%), prediction intervals crossed the null, small-study analyses suggested overestimation, and certainty was very low. Most of 27 local-mediator studies (not pooled) reported higher airway or tonsillar inflammation. Circulating CRP/hs-CRP, TNF-α, and IL-6 are higher in OSA, compatible with hypoxia-driven nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) signaling; heterogeneity, confounding, small-study effects, and very low certainty limit causal inference.

papers.title: Mouth Breathing and STOP-Bang Questionnaire Findings in Adults with Transfusion-Dependent β-Thalassemia: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Chronic anemia and craniofacial changes associated with transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia (TDT) may influence upper airway function and occlusal development. However, evidence regarding mouth breathing, STOP-Bang questionnaire findings, and associated occlusal characteristics in adults with TDT remains limited. To investigate associations between mouth breathing and STOP-Bang questionnaire findings while exploring malocclusion characteristics and other oral functional features among adults with TDT. We conducted a cross-sectional study that included 153 adults with TDT. STOP-Bang classified OSA screening risk; clinical examinations and interviews assessed dentofacial, functional, and patient-reported characteristics. Group comparisons used chi-square or exact tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Firth-penalized logistic regression evaluated a three-item score comprising snoring, observed apnea, and high blood pressure, modeling open bite and mouth breathing as outcomes. Models adjusted for age, sex, BMI, and hemoglobin, followed by mutual adjustment for the other oral feature. Adjusted full-score models were retained as sensitivity analyses. Significance was set at p < 0.05 or FDR-adjusted q < 0.05. Among 153 adults, 113 (73.9%) had low STOP-Bang scores and 40 (26.1%) scored ≥3. Vertical occlusal relationships differed between groups (q = 0.033), with open bite observed in 30.0% versus 12.4%. Mouth breathing was more frequent in the higher-score group (80.0% versus 35.4%; q < 0.001). In exploratory reduced-score analyses, open bite was associated with higher scores after core adjustment (aOR 1.68, 95% CI 1.04-2.75; p = 0.036). The estimate attenuated following additional adjustment for mouth breathing (aOR 1.50, 95% CI 0.86-2.58; p = 0.147), while mouth breathing remained associated after adjustment for open bite (aOR 3.40, 95% CI 2.08-5.95). Among adults with TDT, mouth breathing was associated with STOP-Bang questionnaire findings, while vertical occlusal relationships differed between score groups. Anterior open bite showed a significant association in the core-adjusted reduced-score model, which attenuated following adjustment for mouth breathing without excluding an association. Objective sleep assessments are needed to clarify the clinical significance of these findings.

papers.title: Monitoring Reduced Vigilance Using an Eyeglass-Type EEG System.
papers.abstract: An eyeglass-type electroencephalography (EEG) device has emerged as a promising platform for continuous cognitive state monitoring owing to its seamless integration into daily life and greater usability compared with conventional headset-style EEG systems. However, the feasibility of EEG-based reduced-vigilance monitoring using this form factor remains insufficiently examined. To address this issue, we conducted a two-phase experiment involving 21 participants to establish a mental fatigue-sensitive index and validate a monitoring algorithm for reduced vigilance associated with drowsiness or mental fatigue using a custom-made eyeglass-type EEG device. In the first phase, a long-term sustained attention task (d2 test) was employed to induce mental fatigue, and the ratio of low-alpha to high-beta power was identified as a potential biomarker of mental-fatigue-related vigilance decline. In the second phase, system performance was evaluated through a prolonged, monotonous video-watching experiment designed to elicit reduced vigilance. The algorithm combined the drowsiness detection index (theta-plus-alpha power) from the TP9 and TP10 channels with the candidate fatigue-sensitive index from the differential channel. Subject-specific calibration-based thresholds were used to generate index-specific segment-level decisions, which were combined using a logical OR rule. In the pseudo-real-time evaluation of 16 participants, the final fusion model achieved a mean accuracy of 70.31%, a false-positive rate of 10.40%, a recall of 49.67%, and a precision of 81.80%, calculated from participant-level metrics. Detection performance depended partly on the inclusion of segments with prolonged eye closure, with lower recall after their exclusion. Nevertheless, these findings provide preliminary evidence for the feasibility of detecting behaviorally defined reduced vigilance using an eyeglass-type EEG device.

papers.title: Effects of Baseline Correction Strategy on Cervical Raman Spectral Analysis in a Late-Gestation Rat Model.
papers.abstract: Fluorescence background is a persistent limitation in quantitative Raman spectroscopy of biological tissue, and it is pronounced in the pregnant cervix, where weak Raman bands sit on a strong and variable baseline. Baseline correction is a routine step, yet its effect on the final result is rarely tested in a controlled way. We examined how the choice of correction strategy affects spectral metrics and the biological difference inferred between two gestational stages. Ex vivo cervical spectra from a rat model at gestational days 15 and 20 were processed with fixed-degree polynomial fitting from the second to seventh degrees, five-point piecewise linear correction, an automated polynomial routine, and asymmetric least squares. Correction quality was assessed by the ratio of Raman-active to -inactive regions and by whether each method preserved the direction of gestational change. The choice of method altered the quantitative output and, for some methods, reversed the inferred direction, because the automated high degree of fit over-suppressed the spectrum and inflated the metric. Moderate-degree polynomial fitting and asymmetric least squares gave the most coherent and biologically consistent results. Baseline correction therefore determines cervical Raman outputs and should be selected and reported transparently.

papers.title: Adaptation and Pilot Testing of a Mindfulness-Based Insomnia and Symptom Management Intervention for Women with Breast Cancer in Rural Areas.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is prevalent during breast cancer and exacerbates other common symptoms such as fatigue, distress, and pain, which in turn worsen sleep. This symptom burden is disproportionate for women receiving treatment in rural areas. Nite2Day is a mindfulness-based, behavioral insomnia and symptom management intervention previously applied in hematologic cancer. We adapted and pilot-tested Nite2Day in patients with breast cancer in rural areas. Patient (N = 8) and clinician (N = 6) interviews informed adaptation. A single-arm pilot (N = 15) evaluated feasibility (accrual, attrition, adherence), acceptability, and changes to patient-reported outcomes (insomnia symptoms, fatigue, distress, pain, pre-sleep arousal, mindfulness, symptom management self-efficacy) from baseline to post-intervention. Participants were enthusiastic about mindfulness and behavioral skills to address symptoms. Qualitative feedback guided protocol changes (e.g., mindfulness definitions, telephone and evening sessions). Nite2Day was feasible. The accrual target was met in 6 months, and all participants completed the intervention and post-treatment assessments. Acceptability of Nite2Day was strong (M = 30.53/32). Pre-post change for all patient-reported outcomes was in the expected direction. These feasibility and acceptability data provide support for next-step pilot testing using a randomized design. This research could extend access to an evidence-based behavioral intervention targeting concurrent insomnia, fatigue, distress, and pain symptoms reported by patients in rural cancer care settings.

papers.title: Subjective and Objective Sleep Quality and Associated Factors in Patients with Cancer During Particle Therapy: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Sleep quality during particle therapy remains understudied. We assessed subjective and objective sleep quality, their correlations, and associated factors. This single-center cross-sectional study included 443 patients assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and seven-day wrist actigraphy. Spearman correlations and multivariable logistic regression were used. Among 443 patients, 229 (51.7%) had subjective poor sleep quality and 269 (60.7%) had objective poor sleep quality. Corresponding PSQI and actigraphy-derived sleep measures showed positive Spearman correlations for total sleep time (TST) (ρ = 0.417, p < 0.001), sleep efficiency (SE) (ρ = 0.360, p < 0.001), and sleep-onset latency (SOL) (ρ = 0.273, p < 0.001). In the multivariable model for subjective poor sleep quality, older age (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 1.039 per year; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.013-1.067; p = 0.004), greater symptom burden (aOR = 1.044 per ESAS-r Cancer point; 95% CI, 1.016-1.073; p = 0.002), and hypnotic medication use before particle therapy (aOR = 4.040 versus no use; 95% CI, 1.496-10.909; p = 0.006) were associated with higher odds, whereas healthier sleep beliefs were associated with lower odds (aOR = 0.907 per DBAS-16 point; 95% CI, 0.882-0.933; p < 0.001). Annual household income was also associated with subjective poor sleep quality (overall p = 0.043); specifically, patients earning CNY 200,000-500,000 had higher odds than those earning less than CNY 200,000 (aOR = 2.165; 95% CI, 1.160-4.042; p = 0.015). In the model for objective poor sleep quality, older age (aOR = 1.032 per year; 95% CI, 1.011-1.053; p = 0.003), greater symptom burden (aOR = 1.028 per ESAS-r Cancer point; 95% CI, 1.005-1.052; p = 0.015), and male sex (aOR = 1.904 versus female sex; 95% CI, 1.123-3.230; p = 0.017) were associated with higher odds, while healthier sleep beliefs were associated with lower odds (aOR = 0.979 per DBAS-16 point; 95% CI, 0.959-0.999; p = 0.044). Subjective and objective poor sleep quality were common during particle therapy. Questionnaire screening supplemented by actigraphy may support more comprehensive sleep-quality assessment in oncology nursing.

papers.title: Craniofacial Skeletal and Dentoalveolar Morphology in Bruxism: A Systematic Review of Imaging-Based and Morphometric Observational Studies.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: This systematic review evaluated whether craniofacial skeletal, mandibular and dentoalveolar morphology differs between individuals with and without bruxism. Methods: The protocol was prospectively registered (Open Science Framework) and the review follows PRISMA 2020. MEDLINE (PubMed) was searched from inception to 1 September 2026, supplemented by web, directory, reference-list and forward-citation searches; no other bibliographic database was searched. Two reviewers independently screened records and appraised quality with the JBI checklist. Because heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis, findings were synthesised narratively, with an exploratory effect-direction synthesis for the gonial angle stratified by diagnostic grade, age, temporomandibular disorder status and confounder control. Results: Sixteen studies (1387 participants, ten countries) were included; two used instrumental (definite) bruxism assessment. No consistent association was found with sagittal or vertical skeletal pattern, facial type or headform. Three adult imaging studies with non-instrumental diagnosis reported smaller gonial angles in bruxers (approximately 4° in two), and a fourth reported a reduction confined to women; no reduction was observed in either instrumental study or in any study with age-comparable groups not selected for temporomandibular disorder. Dentoalveolar findings were isolated and inconsistent. Conclusions: The evidence is insufficient to establish a characteristic craniofacial pattern or a reproducible gonial-angle association in bruxism; the reported differences are vulnerable to diagnostic misclassification and confounding. Craniofacial morphology alone should not be used to diagnose bruxism or to guide treatment decisions.

papers.title: Paediatric hypothalamic obesity: clinical phenotype, assessment and emerging treatments.
papers.abstract: Hypothalamic obesity is a severe, treatment-resistant neuroendocrine complication of structural or functional injury to hypothalamic networks, most often following childhood craniopharyngioma or other suprasellar disorders. Rapid weight gain may coexist with hyperphagia, reduced resting energy expenditure, hypersomnolence, pituitary hormone deficiencies, autonomic dysfunction and neurobehavioural morbidity. This clinical review synthesises the current evidence, with an emphasis on paediatric presentation, assessment and management. Hypothalamic obesity reflects disruption of interconnected melanocortin, autonomic, circadian and reward pathways rather than failure of a single appetite centre. The extent and location of hypothalamic injury, particularly posterior involvement, influence clinical severity. Assessment should, therefore, extend beyond body mass index to include weight trajectory, appetite, measured or suspected reductions in energy expenditure, sleep, endocrine status, cognition, behaviour, autonomic function and cardiometabolic risk. Management combines prevention of avoidable hypothalamic injury, physiological pituitary hormone replacement, structured nutritional and behavioural support, adapted physical activity, sleep and neuropsychological care and treatment of comorbidity. Pharmacotherapy may be guided by the dominant phenotype. Glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists may benefit selected patients, while controlled phase 3 evidence and subsequent regulatory approval have established melanocortin 4 receptor (MC4R) agonism with setmelanotide as the first disease-specific treatment for acquired hypothalamic obesity in adults and children aged 4 years and older. Paediatric hypothalamic obesity should be managed as a chronic neuroendocrine disorder within the broader hypothalamic syndrome, rather than as isolated excess weight. Longer-term studies should define treatment durability, age-specific safety, predictors of response, equitable access, and outcomes that matter to children and families, including hunger, wakefulness, participation, behaviour and caregiver burden.
papers.journal: Journal of pediatric endocrinology & metabolism : JPEM

papers.title: Mutation E300 recommended by protein language models gives ChrimsonR amplified photocurrent response.
papers.abstract: A central challenge in rhodopsin engineering is identifying mutations that reliably improve desired functional properties, a task made difficult by the enormous mutation space and limited throughput of electrophysiological screening. Improving rhodopsin properties such as photocurrent amplitude and light sensitivity have the potential to broaden the use of rhodopsins to low-light and deep-tissue applications. With this goal, we applied zero-shot protein language models (ESM-1b/1v) to recommend ChrimsonR mutations and experimentally validated all 17 of these variants using whole-cell patch clamp electrophysiology (n=6 cells per mutation). Despite many mutations reducing function, protein language models identified both known functional residues and unconventional substitutions that produced large functional gains and synergized with K176R to accelerate channel closing. Two mutations, E300G and E300P, increased sustained photocurrents from 66 pA (control) to 305 pA and 255 pA at 635 nm, reduced [Formula: see text] at 575 nm from 0.19 mW to 0.07 mW, and altered kinetics ([Formula: see text] increased from 0.06 s up to 0.40 s relative to ChrimsonR). Our results suggest that protein language models, even without task-specific training, can be used alongside electrophysiological measurements as a strategy for screening rhodopsins for enhanced photocurrent.

papers.title: Yoda molecules agonize PIEZO2.
papers.abstract: Mammalian PIEZO proteins (PIEZO1 and PIEZO2) act as essential mechanosensitive channels. PIEZO1 is thought to be selectively activated by Yoda molecules (Yoda1 and Yoda2). Although a molecular mechanism for PIEZO1 activation by Yoda1 exists, the origin of Yoda1 selective agonism remains obscure. Here, using electrophysiology and calcium imaging in transfected cells, we show that Yoda1 agonizes PIEZO2, but with a distinct efficacy profile compared to PIEZO1. Yoda1 increases single-channel open probability and macroscopic stretch sensitivity of PIEZO2 currents as efficaciously as reported for PIEZO1, but it elicits weak PIEZO2-dependent calcium influx in the absence of external stimulus, an effect detectable only under non-physiological conditions. Yoda1 slows down inactivation of indentation-evoked PIEZO2 currents, but to a lower extent compared to PIEZO1. The Yoda1 analog Dooku1, which does not modulate PIEZO1, slows down PIEZO2 inactivation similarly to Yoda1. Two PIEZO1 agonists unrelated to Yoda1 but thought to populate the same binding site in PIEZO1 have no effect on PIEZO2 inactivation, suggesting that their PIEZO1 selectivity is better than Yoda1. PIEZO2 inactivation is also modulated by Yoda1's more potent analog Yoda2. Using mutagenesis and molecular dynamics simulations, we show that Yoda2's benzoic acid group forms a transient salt-bridge with a conserved arginine in the Yoda binding site (R1724/R2029 in mouse PIEZO1/PIEZO2), explaining the higher potency of this analog for both channels. Together, our study re-evaluates the PIEZO1 selectivity of Yoda molecules and highlights a complex modulatory landscape toward distinct functional properties of PIEZO channels.

papers.title: Longitudinal utility of the Berlin questionnaire to assess obstructive sleep apnea risk: a sequence analysis approach.
Cognitive Performance in Experienced Dancers: A Virtual Reality Comparative Analysis.
papers.abstract: Dance is a complex activity that integrates motor, sensory, and cognitive processes and requires rapid responses, attentional control, and precise sensorimotor integration. Virtual reality (VR) may provide an immersive approach for assessing cognitive performance in contexts relevant to dance. This study aimed to compare reaction time (RT), decision time (DT), attention (AT), and inhibitory control (IC) between experienced dancers and non-dancers using an immersive VR assessment. This cross-sectional study included 26 participants: 13 experienced dancers (9 women, 4 men; 22.15 ± 3.69 years) and 13 non-dancers (9 women, 4 men; 24.15 ± 2.85 years). Cognitive performance was assessed using the NeuroSport Arena VR system, which included simple reaction time and Go/No-Go tasks. Between-group comparisons were performed using the Mann-Whitney U test, with rank-biserial correlation used to estimate effect size. Levene's test assessed differences in variability, and kurtosis was calculated for RT. Exploratory multiple regression analyses examined associations between cognitive outcomes and disposition, mood, sleep quality, and tension. No statistically significant between-group differences were observed for RT, DT, AT, or IC (P > .05). However, experienced dancers demonstrated significantly lower RT variability than non-dancers (F = 5.63, P = .026), with a moderate rank-biserial correlation for RT (.314) and a trend toward faster responses (256.30 ± 18.70 vs 280.15 ± 45.25 ms; P = .091). Exploratory regression analyses showed that tension was associated with AT in dancers (P = .0037), whereas disposition was associated with RT (P = .0424) and AT (P = .0147) in non-dancers. Experienced dancers exhibited greater consistency in reaction time performance and a trend toward faster responses, despite no significant differences in overall cognitive outcomes. These findings suggest that long-term dance practice may be associated with more stable sensorimotor processing and support immersive VR as a promising tool for cognitive assessment in dancers.
authors: Luciane Aparecida Pascucci Sande de Souza
papers.journal: Journal of dance medicine & science : official publication of the International Association for Dance Medicine & Science

papers.title: The Orexinergic System in Alzheimer's Disease: From Sleep Disruption to Accelerated Neurodegeneration.
papers.abstract: Sleep-wake dysregulation is increasingly recognized as an early and clinically relevant feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD), with growing evidence supporting a bidirectional relationship between disturbed sleep and AD pathophysiology. Sleep fragmentation and reduced slow-wave and REM sleep may contribute to amyloid-β (Aβ) accumulation by increasing Aβ production during wakefulness and diminishing glymphatic clearance during sleep, while emerging amyloid pathology can further disrupt sleep architecture and circadian sleep-wake rhythm, reinforcing a feed-forward cycle. Within this framework, the orexinergic system, centered in the hypothalamus and crucial for arousal and sleep-wake stability, has been implicated as a mechanistic link between hyperarousal, impaired sleep consolidation, and altered amyloid dynamics. Preclinical studies suggested that orexin-A signaling can exacerbate Aβ and tau pathology and impair synaptic function, whereas biomarker studies reported high cerebrospinal fluid orexin-A levels in mild cognitive impairment and dementia due to AD. These observations raise the hypothesis that targeting orexin signaling and improving sleep may represent actionable strategies within the AD continuum. Clinical evidence indicates that behavioral and pharmacological interventions can improve sleep in at-risk populations, yet robust proof of disease-modifying effects on AD biomarkers or clinical progression remains limited. Ongoing trials of dual orexin receptor antagonists may clarify whether sustained modulation of sleep-wake regulation can influence AD-related biology beyond symptomatic sleep benefits.

papers.title: Prevalence and Functional Impact of Temporomandibular Disorders in Orthognathic Surgery Candidates and Healthy Controls: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Dentofacial deformities may be associated with temporomandibular disorders (TMDs), but their relationship with pain-related and functional aspects of TMD remains unclear. This study compared patients scheduled for bimaxillary orthognathic surgery with healthy controls in terms of TMD prevalence, oral parafunctions, pain catastrophizing and sleep quality. Forty-five orthognathic surgery candidates and 50 healthy volunteers underwent DC/TMD Axis I examination and completed DC/TMD Axis II questionnaires, including the Oral Behaviour Checklist (OBC), Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7), Graded Chronic Pain Scale (GCPS), 20-item Jaw Functional Limitation Scale (JFLS-20) and additionally the Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and the Fonseca Anamnestic Index (FAI). The prevalence of pain-related TMD (myalgia and/or arthralgia), oral parafunctional behaviours, pain catastrophizing and sleep disturbances did not differ significantly between groups. In contrast, intra-articular TMD was more frequent in the orthognathic surgery group (55.6% vs. 20.0%; OR = 5.00, 95% CI 2.02-12.41; p < 0.001). Orthognathic surgery candidates reported greater jaw functional limitation (JFLS-20: 23.29 ± 25.02 vs. 5.48 ± 9.94; Hedges' g = 0.95; p < 0.001). Orthognathic surgery candidates had a higher prevalence of intra-articular TMD and greater jaw functional limitation than controls. No statistically significant between-group difference in the prevalence of pain-related TMD was detected. Exploratory FAI analyses showed stronger associations with selected clinical pain variables in the orthognathic surgery group, supporting comprehensive preoperative assessment.

papers.title: Machine Learning-Based Development and Longitudinal Validation of a Brief Risk-Stratification Model for Fear of Progression in Patients With Cancer.
papers.abstract: Fear of progression (FOP) is a common and clinically important source of psychological distress in patients with cancer, but comprehensive screening is difficult to implement in busy oncology wards. We examined whether routinely available admission indicators could support early risk stratification for clinically significant FOP. Data were drawn from a multicenter prospective study conducted in nine tertiary hospitals across seven regions of China. The admission sample included 9224 hospitalized patients with cancer, of whom 2146 completed a pre-discharge assessment. Clinically significant FOP was defined as a Fear of Progression Questionnaire-Short Form score ≥ 34. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression was used to derive 30-item and 15-item feature sets from 51 admission variables. Five supervised learning algorithms were trained and evaluated using internal and longitudinal validation. Model performance was assessed using discrimination, calibration, and decision curve analyses. The models showed good discrimination for FOP at admission. Random forest performed best using the full 51-item pool (AUROC = 0.906, 95% CI 0.892-0.919), while the 15-item random forest model retained comparable performance (AUROC = 0.904, 95% CI 0.888-0.917). In the longitudinal validation, admission-based prediction of pre-discharge FOP remained acceptable (best AUROC = 0.827, 95% CI 0.777-0.869). Among the 1778 patients who completed follow-up and did not meet the FOP criterion at admission, 171 (9.62%) met the criterion before discharge. For recent-onset pre-discharge FOP, the corresponding random forest model using the full item pool achieved an AUROC of 0.737 (95% CI 0.663-0.809). Calibration and decision curve analyses supported potential clinical utility. Key predictors included depressive symptoms, sleep-related impairment, fatigue, younger age, region, and primary cancer site. A brief machine learning model based on routine admission data identified hospitalized patients with cancer at risk for clinically significant FOP with strong internal performance and acceptable longitudinal robustness. This approach may facilitate timely psychological risk stratification in oncology wards and support stepped psycho-oncology care.

papers.title: Safety and efficacy of irrigated-tip catheter ablation guided by three-dimensional electroanatomic mapping for atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia: the WATER ATTAC study.

papers.title: Association of Sleep Quality, Perceived Stress, and Dyspnea Among University Students: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: ObjectivesTo examine the associations of sleep quality with perceived stress and perceived dyspnea among Palestinian university students and to assess the incremental contribution of these factors to sleep quality beyond age, gender, and body mass index (BMI).MethodsA cross-sectional study was conducted among 243 university students aged 18-25 years, of whom 66.3% were female. Data were collected using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10), and Modified Borg Dyspnea Scale (mBDS). Descriptive analyses, inferential tests, Spearman's correlation, and hierarchical multiple linear regression were performed, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05.ResultsPoor sleep quality was reported by 69.1% of participants, and mean perceived stress was 18.87 ± 7.33, indicating moderate stress. Perceived stress and mBDS scores were positively associated with Global PSQI scores and with each other (p ≤ .007). Participants with poor sleep quality also reported significantly higher stress and mBDS scores (p < .05). In the final regression model, perceived stress (β = .251) and mBDS scores (β = .240) were independently associated with poorer sleep quality (p < .001), explaining 14.9% of the variance (R2 = .149; adjusted R2 = .131; F (5, 237) = 8.315, p < .001).ConclusionPoor sleep quality was prevalent among Palestinian university students, and perceived stress and perceived dyspnea were independently associated with poorer sleep quality. These findings highlight the need for student sleep health initiatives addressing stress management and breathing-related symptoms. Longitudinal studies using objective assessments are needed to clarify these relationships.
papers.journal: Journal of primary care & community health

papers.title: Footwear-Related Modulation of Scalp EEG Theta/Alpha Ratio During Walking in Children: An Exploratory Within-Subject Study.
papers.abstract: Background: Childhood is a critical period for neuromotor development, during which footwear may influence the sensory and mechanical context of walking. This study examined whether footwear condition was associated with changes in scalp-level EEG activity during walking in 37 typically developing children aged 6-7 years. Methods: Participants completed repeated 10 m walking trials under three randomized conditions: barefoot, barefoot-style footwear, and conventional structured footwear. EEG was recorded using a mobile 14-channel Emotiv EPOC X system. The primary outcome was the global Theta/Alpha ratio averaged across scalp electrodes. Results: Footwear condition significantly affected the global Theta/Alpha ratio (F (2,72) = 14.57, p < 0.001). Conventional structured footwear produced higher Theta/Alpha values than both barefoot walking and barefoot-style footwear, whereas no significant differences were found between barefoot and barefoot-style conditions. Mean paired differences were 1.08 for conventional versus barefoot and 0.99 for conventional versus barefoot-style footwear. Similar directional effects were observed across electrode groupings. No significant differences were identified in absolute theta, alpha, or beta power, global Beta/Alpha ratio, or Shannon entropy. Conclusions: Conventional structured footwear was associated with increased scalp-level Theta/Alpha activity during walking in children, suggesting possible footwear-related modulation of attentional or motor-control demands.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Podiatric Medical Association

papers.title: From Analogue to Digital Experiences: Rethinking Cognitive Reserve in Older Adults.
papers.abstract: The construct of cognitive reserve (CR) has traditionally been grounded in analogue life-course indicators, including years of education, occupational complexity, lifestyle, and cognitively stimulating activities. However, the rapid digital transformation of recent decades has introduced a pervasive environmental factor that may reshape the experiences through which CR is built: sustained interaction with digital technologies. This narrative review examines the emerging relationship between CR and digital experiences, with particular attention to heterogeneity within the older population. We distinguish between older adults whose adult and working lives were predominantly analogue, currently in their eighties, and new older adults, currently in their sixties and seventies, who encountered digital technologies during adulthood and progressively integrated them into their personal and professional lives. Available evidence suggests that engagement with digital environments may be associated with better executive functioning, attention, visuospatial abilities, and memory, although most studies are observational. Existing CR instruments, developed within a predominantly analogue framework, do not systematically capture these experiences. We therefore propose an integrated analogue-digital model of CR, in which digital experiences expand rather than replace traditional reserve dimensions. Within this model, we introduce Digital Cognitive Reserve (DCR) as a framework for assessing digital experiences as possible proxies of reserve and outline four preliminary dimensions (digital exposure, diversity, cognitive complexity, and adaptability), together with testable predictions that may inform future studies and assessment tools. Longitudinal, psychometric, and neurobiological studies are needed to test whether digital experiences contribute to cognitive resilience and to guide technology-based interventions tailored to cohort-specific profiles.

papers.title: Single- and Multi-SNP Genotype Analyses of the Circadian-Related SLC20A2 Gene Reveal Sex-Specific Associations with Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD).
papers.abstract: Circadian clock gene variants have been linked to mood disorders, including seasonal affective disorder (SAD), suggesting that molecular pathways affecting seasonal mood are influenced by the circadian clock and sleep-wake patterns, but the molecular mechanisms underlying these links are poorly understood. Building on animal and human evidence that SLC20A2 influences seasonal circadian adaptation, we tested associations between five SLC20A2 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and symptoms of SAD and depression. We examined both single-SNP and multi-SNP genotypes in a deeply phenotyped undergraduate population and assessed whether these associations differed by sex. Seasonality scores were strongly associated with differences in seasonal sleep duration in this population. Three SNPs (rs6988483, rs13281070, rs3763510) were significantly associated with self-reported SAD symptom severity, with the effects of SLC-3 and SLC-4 concentrated in males. Multi-SNP genotype analysis identified eight multi-SNP combinations associated with self-reported SAD. One risk genotype conferred roughly nine times greater odds of SAD symptoms in females, and this genotype and two protective genotypes showed no corresponding association with general depressive symptoms, suggesting these variants influence seasonal depression specifically, rather than depressive symptoms broadly. Five additional genotypes were protective against both SAD and depression. These findings provide initial evidence that SLC20A2 variation, at both the single-SNP and genotype level, may contribute to SAD risk in a sex-specific manner and that a subset of this variation may act on seasonal mood regulation independent of general depression risk. Our results support SLC20A2 as a candidate gene for circadian-related mood disorders and point to potential new therapeutic targets, though replication in larger, sex-balanced cohorts is needed.

papers.title: Mitigating Sleep Inertia and Maintaining Neurobehavioral Performance in Shift Workers via Multisensory (Music and Light) Intervention: A Preliminary Field Study.
papers.abstract: Irregular shift schedules in railway operations increase safety risks through fatigue and sleep inertia. We evaluated a wearable multisensory device that delivers sleep-promoting music in darkness before sleep and uplifting music with blue light upon awakening. In a preliminary field crossover study, 17 railway staff completed the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT), Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS), and Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) before and after on-duty sleep, with and without the device. In a separate electroencephalography (EEG) study, 10 healthy adults received sleep-onset and wake-up stimulation while EEG was recorded at Fz, Cz, and Pz. Compared to the control condition, the intervention maintained PVT response speed, reduced lapses at the end of the shift, and was associated with longer sleep duration. The PVT results, but not positive affect, remained significant after adjustment for pre-sleep values. Sleepiness was not significantly reduced overall and was lower only in an exploratory station subgroup. In the EEG study, the slow-to-fast power ratio increased during sleep-onset stimulation, and theta power was transiently lower early in wake-up stimulation than at the end of sleep-onset stimulation. These preliminary findings suggest that dual-phase multisensory stimulation may help sustain alertness in shift workers, although larger sham-controlled trials are needed.

papers.title: Poor Sleep Quality and the Prevalence of Intrinsic Capacity Impairments Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Introduction: Sleep quality has been associated with cognitive, psychological, and physical outcomes in older adults; however, its relationship with intrinsic capacity (IC) as a multidimensional construct remains insufficiently understood. Objective: Our objective was to investigate the association between sleep quality and overall IC and its individual domains in community-dwelling older adults. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 477 physically independent community-dwelling adults. Sleep quality was assessed using the Brazilian Portuguese version of the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. The five IC domains were assessed using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, 15-item Geriatric Depression Scale, Short Physical Performance Battery, Snellen chart and Whispered Voice Test, and Mini Nutritional Assessment. Domain scores were combined into an overall IC score ranging from 0 to 10. Overall IC and each domain were classified as preserved or impaired. Associations were examined using Poisson regression. Results: The largest association was observed for psychological impairment (PR = 1.97; 95% CI: 1.23-3.84), followed by locomotor impairment (PR = 1.32; 95% CI: 1.02-1.77). Smaller estimates were observed for overall IC (PR = 1.16; 95% CI: 0.99-1.36) and sensory impairment (PR = 1.14; 95% CI: 0.99-1.32), with confidence intervals including the null value. Little evidence of association was found for cognitive or vitality impairment. Conclusions: Poor sleep quality was associated with a higher prevalence of psychological and locomotor impairment. However, overlapping confidence intervals and the absence of formal comparisons between outcomes preclude concluding that the associations differ across IC domains.

papers.title: Usability and Acceptability of Digital Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Insomnia (Sleepio) in People with Cognitive Impairment: A Mixed-Methods Study.
papers.abstract: Insomnia and dementia are major public health issues. Although cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the recommended first line treatment for insomnia, few studies have examined its usability or effectiveness in people with cognitive impairment. Digital CBT-I (dCBT-I) is an effective and easily accessible alternative to CBT-I. We undertook a mixed-methods analysis of the usability and acceptability of dCBT-I (SleepioTM) in patients attending a memory clinic. Participants were community dwellers aged ≥50 years with insomnia (Sleep Condition Indicator score ≤ 16) and subjective cognitive decline (SCD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or dementia. The Mobile Device Proficiency Questionnaire (MDPQ) assessed digital literacy. The System Usability Score (SUS) and Usability Metric for User Experience-Lite (UMUX-Lite) assessed usability. Acceptability was assessed by analysing adherence to the intervention and subjective reports of perceived benefit. Both usability and acceptability were further explored in semi-structured interviews. Among 24 participants (median age 69; 17 females), 2 had SCD, 14 MCI, and 8 dementia. Overall response to SleepioTM was positive. Participants favoured relaxation-based aspects of the programme. Behavioural elements, such as sleep restriction, were generally less favoured. Lack of digital literacy was the main barrier to engagement, though this could be surmounted by assistance from caregivers or family members in certain instances. Regardless of cognitive status, those with above-average digital literacy (MDPQ > 20) undertook a median 6/6 sessions, while those with below-average digital literacy (MDPQ < 20) undertook a median 3/6 sessions. Among those with above-average digital literacy, median SUS and UMUX-Lite were 72.5 and 75, respectively, representing acceptable usability, while overall scores were 63.75 and 56.25, respectively, representing marginally acceptable usability. Our findings may suggest that SleepioTM is usable and acceptable for people with SCD, MCI and selected individuals with mild dementia, particularly where digital literacy is preserved. Additional caregiver support may facilitate usability among people with MCI and lower digital literacy. Usability appears limited in more advanced dementia. However, as some subgroups were small, more research is required to confirm these findings.

papers.title: Adverse Childhood Experiences and Metabolic Risk: Differential Associations with Metabolic and Circadian Syndromes from the CHARLS National Cohort.
papers.abstract: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are associated with neurodevelopment, emotional regulation, circadian rhythms, and physiological homeostasis, exerting lifelong effects on both psychological and physical health. Individuals exposed to ACEs have a higher risk of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease than the general population. We screened for high-risk ACEs and determined their associations with circadian syndrome (CircS) and metabolic syndrome (MetS) using data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS). Based on the 20 ACE indicators identified in previous research, we coded two additional indicators and performed univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses to examine the associations of individual ACE indicators with CircS and MetS. After using LASSO regression to screen for high-risk ACEs for the two syndromes, we conducted a mutually exclusive combination analysis. Illness-related school absence, bed rest, or hospitalization was associated with the highest increased prevalence for CircS, with odds ratios (ORs) of 1.27 (1.10, 1.46). For MetS, parental anxiety/depression symptoms were the only ACE indicator showing a statistically significant inverse association. For the ACE combinations, associations with the two syndromes were only observed for specific ACE combinations. Notably, the combination of parental anxiety/depressive symptoms, poor parent-child relationship, parental favoritism, and childhood food insecurity/starvation significantly increased the prevalence of both CircS and MetS, with ORs of 3.63 (1.39, 9.50) for CircS and 3.01 (1.13, 7.96) for MetS. ACE indicators and their combinations confer an elevated prevalence of CircS and MetS in the Chinese population, with the magnitude of association varying across individual ACEs.

papers.title: Experimental Sleep Manipulation and Pain Sensitivity in Healthy Adults: A Focused Review with Emphasis on Sleep Fragmentation.
papers.abstract: Experimental sleep loss can increase pain sensitivity, but sleep duration, continuity, and architecture are often altered simultaneously. This focused review compared pain outcomes across experimental sleep manipulations in healthy adults, with particular attention to sleep fragmentation (SF) and related awakening paradigms. PubMed and Web of Science Core Collection were searched through 16 September 2026; reference and citation checking identified additional reports. Eligible reports were synthesized narratively by sleep manipulation, design, pain modality, and dynamic pain-processing outcome. Designs included randomized or counterbalanced crossover studies, other within-participant or repeated-measures experiments, and parallel-group studies. Fifty-two reports met the eligibility criteria. After overlapping and nested publications were consolidated, they formed 40 publication families comprising 41 provisionally distinct participant samples and approximately 1083 participants with analyzable data. Non-mutually exclusive categories comprised 21 reports of total sleep deprivation (TSD) or prolonged wakefulness, 17 of partial sleep restriction (PSR) or night-shift exposure, two directly evaluating SF, 10 evaluating related planned- or forced-awakening paradigms, six evaluating selective sleep-stage disruption, and two reports from provisionally distinct samples evaluating combined short and disrupted sleep. TSD and PSR showed the broadest evidence of increased pain sensitivity, but effects varied by modality and outcome. Both direct-SF reports identified at least one hyperalgesic outcome; the awakening literature was suggestive but contained multiple reports from shared samples. The combined protocol did not isolate sleep continuity from reduced duration. Disrupted sleep continuity may contribute to hyperalgesia, but an independent effect of SF remains uncertain because direct evidence is limited and awakening protocols often also change sleep duration, architecture, stress, or circadian timing.

papers.title: The Gap Between Subjective Sleep Complaints and Objective Obstructive Sleep Apnea Burden Among Professional Drivers.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is highly relevant among professional drivers; however, self-reported symptoms may not reflect the objective disease burden. This cross-sectional study examined the relationship between subjective sleep complaints and the objectively measured OSA burden in 207 professional metropolitan public transport drivers undergoing respiratory polygraphy. Daytime sleepiness, insomnia symptoms, sleep quality, and OSA risk were assessed using the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and STOP-BANG questionnaire. The objective OSA burden was assessed using the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) and the sleep apnea-specific hypoxic burden (SASHB). Moderate-to-severe OSA (AHI ≥ 15 events/h) was identified in 65.2% of participants, whereas excessive daytime sleepiness was reported by only 2.4%. The ESS, AIS, and PSQI scores were correlated with one another but not with the AHI or SASHB. A model combining these subjective measures showed limited discrimination for moderate-to-severe OSA (area under the curve [AUC] = 0.533), whereas a model including age and body mass index (BMI) showed modest discrimination (AUC = 0.637), with BMI independently associated with the outcome. Subjective sleep complaints were poorly associated with the objectively measured OSA burden, supporting the use of clinical risk assessment and objective sleep evaluation when indicated.

papers.title: Which Blood Pressure Measures Correlate with Nocturia Severity in Adolescents?
papers.abstract: Nocturia, defined as waking to void during sleep hours, is common in adolescents, causing sleep disruption and daytime fatigue. While numerous studies have found nocturia associated with systolic blood pressure (BP) hypertension in adults, diastolic (D) BP has greater relative importance in youth. Little is known about the hemodynamic profile of the hypertension-nocturia link in adolescents. Accordingly, we evaluated relationships between nocturia severity and brachial artery systolic and DBPs in each arm, as well as central aortic pressures using applanation tonometry. We studied 100 adolescents, 10-18 years, from pediatric clinics. Nocturnal urinary indices were obtained from voiding diaries. Results: In total, 45% reported nocturia. Nocturia severity was correlated with left and right arm brachial SBP, higher of two arms, and central SBP (r = 0.27, p = 0.007). Brachial SBP was also correlated with nocturnal urine volume (NUV) (r = 0.31, p = 0.001) and production rate (NUP) (r = 0.32, p = 0.001). DBP showed no significant correlations. After adjusting for BMI and sex, brachial SBP remained independently associated with nocturia severity. The median first uninterrupted sleep period was 171 min (25-75%ile; 94, 300). In adolescents, SBP is associated with nocturia severity, NUV, and NUP. Nocturia typically occurs during the first half of nighttime, suggesting an impact on deep sleep.

papers.title: Auditory Steady-State Responses in Adults Aged 88-95 Years Measured in a Home Setting: Feasibility and Agreement with Pure-Tone Audiometry.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Hearing assessment may be challenging in individuals of very advanced age when cognitive or physical limitations restrict participation in behavioural testing or access to clinic-based hearing care. This study evaluated the suitability of auditory steady-state responses (ASSRs) as a clinical method for assessing peripheral hearing in individuals of very advanced age by examining its agreement with pure-tone audiometry (PTA) thresholds and its feasibility in a home setting among individuals aged 88-95 years. Methods: Home visits were conducted for 91 individuals, of whom 71 completed the behavioural and electrophysiological test protocol and were included in the analyses. ASSR thresholds at 0.5, 1, 2, and 4 kHz were compared with corresponding PTA thresholds for the right and left ears. Agreement was assessed using Bland-Altman analyses, with differences within ±15 dB considered clinically acceptable. Reasons for unobtained ASSR thresholds were systematically recorded. The Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) was administered, and PTA-ASSR threshold differences were compared using a cut-off score of ≤26 for cognitive impairment. Results: ASSR thresholds were within ±15 dB of the corresponding PTA thresholds in 92% of right ears and 85% of left ears. Mean differences were close to 0 dB at most frequencies, although greater differences were observed at 0.5 and 1 kHz in the left ear. The mean ASSR test duration was 21.5 min. ASSR thresholds were unobtainable in 31% of PTA-ASSR comparisons, most commonly because of high rejection rates related to EEG and/or myogenic activity and participant discomfort. PTA-ASSR threshold differences did not differ significantly between MMSE groups (≤26 vs. >26). Conclusions: ASSR offers a promising alternative for hearing assessment in individuals of very advanced age who may have difficulty participating in behavioural testing. Furthermore, the results suggest that ASSR can be performed in home settings, including nursing homes and residential care facilities. Participant comfort and positioning are important for reducing muscular artefacts and improving measurement feasibility.

papers.title: Real-World Clinical and Electroencephalographic Outcomes Following Sulthiame Treatment in Children with SeLECTS and SWAS: A Retrospective Study Predominantly Involving Polytherapy.
papers.abstract: Although self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (SeLECTS) generally has a favorable prognosis, some patients experience persistent seizures or develop spike-wave activation in sleep (SWAS). This study evaluated the effectiveness and tolerability of sulthiame in children with SeLECTS, including a small subgroup with accompanying SWAS that preceded sulthiame initiation. This retrospective study evaluated clinical, demographic, EEG, and treatment data from 25 children with SeLECTS treated with sulthiame. Seizure outcomes were assessed at 3-6 and 12 months, and EEG responses were evaluated in patients who developed SWAS. Sulthiame was introduced relatively late in the treatment course (mean age at initiation, 7.2 years; mean treatment line, 3). At 3-6 months, 17 of 21 patients with available outcome data (81%) were seizure-free. Among these 17 patients, 13 (76%) remained seizure-free at 12 months, 2 (12%) experienced seizure recurrence, including one during tapering of a concomitant ASM, and 2 (12%) had no available 12-month outcome data. Using the entire cohort as the denominator (n = 25), documented seizure freedom at 3-6 months was 68% (17/25) and documented sustained seizure freedom through 12 months was 52% (13/25). Sulthiame was administered predominantly as part of polytherapy, with 23 of 25 patients (92%) receiving concomitant ASMs. Favorable seizure and EEG outcomes were observed following sulthiame initiation, predominantly in the context of polytherapy. However, the uncontrolled retrospective design limits attribution of these outcomes specifically to sulthiame and conclusions regarding tolerability. These findings support further evaluation in prospective controlled studies.
