papers.title: Factors Associated with of Parkinson's Disease Knowledge and Attitudes Among Caregivers in Egypt: A Multicenter Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Background: Caregiver awareness and positive attitudes are essential for the early recognition and effective management of Parkinson's disease. This study aimed to examine the factors associated with caregivers' knowledge and attitudes toward the disease. Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among caregivers of patients with Parkinson's disease across three clinical settings in Alexandria, Egypt. A stratified probability sampling technique was used to recruit 383 formal and informal caregivers between 1/2025 and 6/2025. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 23.0. Results: Most of the respondents were females (72.1%), and about half were between 18-30 years (50.9%). Generally, the participants had generally low knowledge and positive attitudes toward PD. The mean knowledge score was 4.52 ± 1.37 out of 10 and the mean attitude score was 27.62 ± 3.49 out of the maximum score of 35. Several key characteristics were significantly associated with knowledge levels. Marital status was significantly associated with knowledge scores. Unmarried participants had higher knowledge scores (mean rank = 221.75). Knowledge score was also associated with educational level, monthly income, household type and primary source of information (p < 0.05 for all); after false discovery rate correction, marital status, household type and source of information remained significant. Sleep duration was the only factor associated with attitude scores, with participants reporting more than six hours of sleep per day exhibiting more positive attitudes (mean rank = 201.88 vs. 178.52, p = 0.039); this association did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons. In multiple linear regression, monthly income and marital status were associated with knowledge scores, whereas education level and sleep duration were associated with attitude scores; however, the models explained only 6.4% and 5.1% of the variance, respectively. Conclusions: Caregivers of individuals with PD in Alexandria, Egypt, demonstrated positive attitudes but generally low knowledge of Parkinson's disease. The caregiver characteristics examined explained little of the variation in knowledge and attitudes, so the associations identified should be regarded as exploratory. Existing knowledge gaps and misconceptions highlight the need for targeted educational interventions.

papers.title: Swimming Toward Recovery: Early Aquatic Therapy as a Bridge to Delayed Environmental Enrichment After Experimental Traumatic Brain Injury.
papers.abstract: Environmental enrichment (EE) is a well-established preclinical model of neurorehabilitation after traumatic brain injury (TBI). However, most paradigms initiate EE immediately after injury and provide it continuously, unlike clinical rehabilitation, which is typically delayed until medical stabilization and delivered for defined periods. We hypothesized that early aquatic therapy (AQT), an exercise-based intervention, would enhance the benefits of delayed EE, providing a rehabilitative bridge during the early post-injury period. Adult male rats received a cortical impact or sham injury and were housed under standard (STD) conditions. Beginning 1 day after surgery, bridge groups received daily AQT for 7 days, while comparison groups remained in STD housing. On post-injury day 8, EE (6 h/day) was initiated in bridge and EE-only groups. Motor, cognitive, and anxiety-like behaviors were assessed. AQT alone and AQT + EE improved motor performance versus STD (p < 0.05), with AQT + EE producing the fewest foot slips and outperforming EE alone. EE improved spatial learning, while AQT + EE produced the strongest acquisition among TBI groups (p < 0.05); memory retention improved only in EE-treated groups. AQT + EE outperformed STD on the first and third reversal stages of executive function, whereas EE alone outperformed STD on the third reversal. Reduced anxiety-like behavior occurred only in EE-treated groups. Overall, the hypothesis was partially supported as sequential AQT + EE produced greater improvements than EE alone on selected motor, spatial learning, and executive outcomes, but EE alone improved memory retention and anxiety-like behavior. These findings support early AQT as a rehabilitative bridge to delayed EE and warrant further investigation of staged rehabilitation paradigms after TBI.

papers.title: Adult EEG Reactivity in Rat Offspring After an Uncomplicated Birth Is Not Significantly Altered by Gestational Antibiotics.
papers.abstract: Prolonged gestational antibiotic exposure was previously reported to impair EEG reactivity in adult offspring after perinatal asphyxia. It remained unclear to what extent the effect depended on perinatal insult. We assessed adult EEG reactivity after uncomplicated birth using the same gestational treatment paradigm. Pregnant Wistar rats received antibiotics (AB), probiotics (P), combined treatment (AB&P), or control (C). Adult offspring (AB: 5; P: 8; AB&P: 7; C: 9; 14 males) underwent intermittent photic stimulation during chloral-hydrate-induced EEG burst suppression. Reactivity to 60 s stimulation was quantified in 180 s trials using burst count reactivity (BCR) and the burst-suppression reactivity index (BSRi). After baseline burst count filtering, 200 trials were retained across groups. BCR did not differ significantly between groups. No multiplicity-corrected pairwise comparison identified a specific treatment-associated difference in BCR or BSRi. Mixed-effects models accounting for repeated trials likewise showed no significant overall group effect. Our small cohort did not provide evidence for a long-term effect of gestational antibiotic or probiotic exposure following uncomplicated birth. Together with the previous report, we suggest that gestational antibiotic administration could impair resilience to perinatal asphyxia at an exposure level without a readily detectable effect after uncomplicated birth.

papers.title: So Much Variety, so Much to Eat: The Neuro-Cognitive Bases of Visual Food Categorization in Infancy.
papers.abstract: Food is fundamental to life. Yet, detecting members of the food category raises a substantial cognitive challenge as different foods do not have any apparent common visual features. Moreover, what is deemed edible and appropriate to eat also varies greatly across social groups. While the neuro-cognitive bases of visual food category representations are well documented in adults, their early ontogenetic origins remain unknown. The current study investigated the emergence of visual food categorization abilities in infants' brains, using the fast periodic visual stimulation paradigm (FPVS) coupled with electroencephalography (EEG). In FPVS paradigms, images from a target category are periodically inserted into a rapid stream of base images from other categories. If the brain treats the target images as a distinct category relative to the base images, a distinct EEG response appears at the frequency of presentation of the target images. In our study, French-speaking adults, 12- and 6-month-old infants (n = 25 per age group) were presented with target food stimuli inserted into sequences of base stimuli from various non-food categories (e.g., manmade objects, plants). Results show that, similarly to adults, 12-month-old infants distinguished images of food from those of other categories. In contrast, 6-month-old infants showed no detectable categorization response to food images. The current study is the first to investigate the developmental course of visual food categorization in the human brain and showed that, by their first birthday, infants already group perceptually diverse foods into a single category.

papers.title: Salivary Antioxidant Capacity During Examination Periods in University Students and Before and After a Running Event in Recreational Runners: An Exploratory Repeated-Measures Study.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: This exploratory observational repeated-measures study investigated changes in salivary antioxidant capacity (SAT) in two independent cohorts under distinct real-life conditions: during academic examination periods in university students and following acute exercise in recreational runners. Methods: Nineteen dental students were assessed during an examination period and again during the regular academic term, while 20 recreational runners were assessed before and after participation in a 5, 10, or 21 km running event. SAT was measured using the Salivary Antioxidant Test on a FRAS 5 system, and lifestyle-, sleep-, and physical activity-related variables were examined as secondary exploratory factors. Results: In university students, no statistically significant difference in SAT was detected between the examination period and the regular academic term (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.966), with nearly identical median values (867 and 870 μmol/L, respectively). In recreational runners, SAT increased after exercise in 14 of 20 participants, with a median within-participant change of +241.5 μmol/L; however, the overall pre- to post-exercise difference did not reach statistical significance (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, W = 53.0, exact two-sided p = 0.053), and substantial inter-individual variability was observed. Exploratory analyses suggested associations between SAT and selected physical activity, lifestyle-related, and questionnaire-derived variables. However, no statistically significant association was detected between early awakening and SAT during the examination period (Spearman's ρ = -0.019, p = 0.940). These exploratory findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the small sample sizes and multiple comparisons. Conclusions: Overall, the findings indicate that SAT may vary across academic and exercise-related measurement conditions, though the present data do not establish the underlying physiological mechanisms or the independent effects of psychological stress or habitual physical activity. Larger, adequately powered studies using more standardised conditions and complementary oxidative, inflammatory, and neuroendocrine biomarkers are required to determine the potential utility of SAT for repeated non-invasive monitoring.
papers.journal: Journal of functional morphology and kinesiology

papers.title: Group-Level Cohesion Ratings Across a Fixed-Order Individual-to-Multiplayer Gaming Paradigm: An Exploratory Study.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Comparisons between individual and multiplayer gaming can reflect social context, but in a fixed-order design condition cannot be separated from order-related effects. This exploratory study therefore focused on group-level Group Cohesiveness Scale (GCS) ratings across a sequential paradigm in which individual play always preceded multiplayer play. A study-specific OpenPose posture-consistency metric and a device/software-derived beta-band output from a small EEG subsample were retained only as ancillary exploratory observations. Methods: Sixty healthy young adults (mean age, 21.21 ± 3.07 years) completed the individual condition first and the multiplayer condition second in 10 assigned groups of six, separated by a one-hour break. GCS scores were averaged within each group, yielding 10 paired group-level means. OpenPose recordings from all 60 participants were summarized descriptively because participant-level paired values required for inferential reanalysis were unavailable. One randomly selected participant per group wore a NeuroSky MindWave Mobile 2 device (n = 10); because the exact eegID processing pipeline and artifact-control procedures were not retained, this output was treated only as a device/software-specific ancillary metric. Results: Mean group-level GCS ratings were 18.13 ± 0.55 after the first, individual condition and 23.55 ± 4.17 after the second, multiplayer condition (mean difference, +5.42). The retained statistical summary reported p < 0.0043; because the original SPSS output is unavailable, 0.0043 is treated as an upper bound rather than an exact recoverable p-value. Using the arithmetic mean of the two condition SDs as the standardizer, Cohen's d_av was 2.30. Mean OpenPose posture-consistency scores were 97.13 ± 2.90 and 93.25 ± 6.24, respectively; this comparison is descriptive only. In the ancillary EEG subsample, the retained software-derived beta-band values were 34.55 ± 12.92 and 47.56 ± 15.33 a.u. (p = 0.022; Cohen's d_av = 0.92), but the physiological source of this difference cannot be determined from the available methodology. Conclusions: Within this fixed sequential paradigm, the second, multiplayer condition was accompanied by higher group-level GCS ratings, but the difference cannot be attributed specifically to multiplayer interaction because condition was completely confounded with order, time, familiarization, anticipation, fatigue, and repeated-task effects. The OpenPose and EEG observations remain ancillary and hypothesis-generating and do not support causal, attentional, engagement, or cortical interpretations.
papers.journal: Journal of functional morphology and kinesiology

papers.title: Associations of Free-Living Physical Activity, Sleep, and Wellness with Neuromuscular, Postural, and Visuomotor Performance in University Students: A 14-Day Multimodal Study.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Habitual physical activity, sleep, and psychological wellness may relate to physical and cognitive-motor performance in young adults, but these relationships are seldom examined within one free-living monitoring framework. This study examined associations of daily physical activity, sleep, and wellness with neuromuscular, postural, and visuomotor performance in university students. Methods: In a 14-day prospective observational design, Samsung Health provided daily step totals, while WHO-5, PSS-10, PSQI, and daily wellness measures characterized recovery. OptoJump, GYKO, and BlazePod assessments were repeated across three laboratory sessions. The prespecified analysis cohort comprised 242 students with ≥10 valid monitoring days (including ≥1 weekend day) and ≥2 valid laboratory sessions per outcome. Sex-adjusted linear mixed-effects models included 237 participants and 696 repeated observations, adjusting for session, age, BMI, weekly training volume, academic period, and testing time. Results: Each additional 1000 steps/day was associated with greater countermovement jump height (β = 1.31 cm, 95% CI 0.97-1.65), lower eyes-closed L5 movement velocity (β = -0.65 mm/s, 95% CI -1.00 to -0.30), and faster choice-response time (β = -6.22 ms, 95% CI -9.37 to -3.08; all Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Higher perceived stress and poorer PSQI-defined sleep quality were independently associated with less favorable performance across all three domains, whereas mean self-reported sleep duration was not. Conclusions: Higher habitual step count, lower perceived stress, and better sleep quality were associated with a more favorable multidimensional performance profile. Because step count was summarized at the participant level, these findings should be interpreted as between-participant associations rather than causal or day-to-day readiness effects. Device-source attribution and postural-measure validation remain limitations.
papers.journal: Journal of functional morphology and kinesiology

papers.title: Association Between Collision Exposure and Post-Match Physiological Recovery Markers in Rugby Union Players: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Background: Collision exposure during rugby union matches may influence post-match fatigue and recovery. However, direct evidence linking quantified match-related collision exposure to post-match recovery outcomes is limited. Objective: To systematically review associations between match-related collision exposure and post-match recovery outcomes in rugby union players and distinguish direct evidence from indirect or contextual evidence within the broader review framework. Methods: This review, registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF), followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. PubMed and Scopus were searched (final search: 5 August 2026), with PubMed Central used for full-text retrieval. Studies of rugby union players were eligible, and the direct-evidence studies were all match-based studies in male players from professional or elite amateur settings. Among 605 records identified, 11 studies were retained within the review framework: 4 as direct evidence and 7 as indirect or contextual evidence. Owing to differences in collision exposure definitions, biomarkers, post-match assessment times, and effect measures, evidence was synthesized narratively according to the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis guideline. Results: Four match-based studies (79 enrolled players in total) provided direct evidence for the review question. Three examined biochemical markers associated with muscle damage, specifically creatine kinase, myoglobin, and interstitial creatine kinase, but they differed in collision metrics, specimen types, and post-match sampling windows, which ranged from 30-45 min to 24 and 40 h. Across these studies, higher collision exposure was generally associated with greater post-match perturbation in these muscle-damage-related biochemical responses, although the clearest reported association in Jones et al. was limited to backs and the statistical detail available from Smart et al. was comparatively limited. One small study suggested that greater collision frequency was associated with poorer post-match sleep architecture; however, this finding should be interpreted as preliminary single-study evidence for a recovery-related outcome rather than an established physiological trend. Direct evidence regarding neuromuscular fatigue was insufficient. One indirect study reported increased post-match resting metabolic rate but did not examine its association with quantified collision exposure. Conclusions: Limited direct evidence links collision exposure to post-match recovery-related outcomes. The strongest signal concerns muscle-damage-associated biochemical markers, but this evidence is based on only three heterogeneous studies with limited cross-study comparability. Evidence concerning sleep architecture remains preliminary and is currently based on a single small study. These findings are correlational. Hence, future match-based studies should separate collision exposure from other workload measures and assess recovery-related outcomes across domains at standardized post-match time points.
papers.journal: Journal of functional morphology and kinesiology

papers.title: Exploratory Biopsychosocial Profiles in Adults with Chronic Low Back Pain: A Cluster Analysis of Clinical, Psychological, Sleep, and Physical Characteristics.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Chronic low back pain (CLBP) is a heterogeneous condition shaped by interacting clinical, psychological, sleep-related, physical, and contextual factors. This study aimed to identify exploratory biopsychosocial profiles in adults with CLBP and to examine whether sociodemographic and anthropometric characteristics differed across the identified profiles. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 143 adults with CLBP recruited from healthcare services in northern Ecuador. Nine clinical, psychological, sleep-related, and physical variables were standardized and entered into a cluster analysis. Sociodemographic and anthropometric variables not used to derive the clusters were subsequently examined as external characteristics. Results: Two profiles were identified (Cluster 1, n = 54; Cluster 2, n = 89), with limited internal separation (mean silhouette coefficient = 0.163). The greatest between-profile contrasts were observed for neuropathic-like pain characteristics, pain catastrophizing, and fear-avoidance beliefs, whereas disability and sleep quality contributed comparatively less to profile differentiation. A PD-Q score ≥19 was observed in 9.3% of participants in Cluster 1 and 40.4% in Cluster 2. Cluster membership was significantly associated with educational level (p = 0.006) and place of residence (p < 0.001), whereas no statistically significant association was observed for sex (p = 0.061). Conclusions: These findings provide evidence of multidimensional heterogeneity among adults with CLBP. Difference between profiles appeared to be driven predominantly by neuropathic-like and cognitive-emotional characteristics rather than by pain intensity or disability alone. The limited internal separation suggests that the identified profiles may represent partially overlapping patterns within a broader biopsychosocial continuum rather than discrete clinical subtypes. Independent replication and external validation are required before these profiles can be considered for clinical stratification or treatment decision-making.
papers.journal: Journal of functional morphology and kinesiology

papers.title: Stress and Wound Healing: Biopsychosocial Mechanisms Linking Neuroendocrine Dysregulation to Delayed Tissue Repair-A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Stress is increasingly recognized as a clinically relevant modifier of tissue repair, yet its effects on wound healing cannot be explained by a single endocrine or immune pathway. Psychological distress, pain, surgical trauma, social adversity, sleep disruption, and chronic disease may converge on the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, sympathetic-adrenomedullary signaling, local neurocutaneous pathways, immune-cell function, redox balance, angiogenesis, fibroblast activity, extracellular-matrix turnover, and health-related behaviors. This narrative review examines the biopsychosocial mechanisms through which acute and chronic stress can delay wound healing and discusses the implications for surgical wounds, experimental wounds, and chronic non-healing wounds. A structured narrative search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science and citation tracking of key reviews and primary studies was used, with emphasis on peer-reviewed human, translational, and mechanistic evidence relevant to stress biology and wound repair. Human studies consistently demonstrate that caregiving stress, academic examination stress, hostile interpersonal interactions, elevated perceived stress, and preoperative distress are associated with slower healing or dysregulated local wound mediators. Mechanistically, excessive or poorly regulated glucocorticoid signaling can suppress early pro-inflammatory cytokines, impair leukocyte trafficking, fibroblast proliferation, collagen deposition, angiogenesis, and re-epithelialization, whereas sympathetic activation and catecholamines can alter vascular tone and adrenergic signaling within the wound microenvironment. Stress also influences macrophage function, neuropeptide signaling, oxidative stress, pain, sleep, nutrition, treatment adherence, and social behavior. In chronic wounds, these pathways become bidirectional: the wound itself generates pain, odor, exudate, functional impairment, and social isolation, which can sustain psychological distress and neuroimmune dysregulation. Psychological and behavioral interventions, including relaxation with guided imagery, mindfulness-based approaches, expressive writing, and social support, show promising but heterogeneous effects and should be viewed as adjuncts rather than substitutes for evidence-based wound care. Integrating stress assessment and biopsychosocial management into wound-care pathways may improve recovery, particularly in patients with high psychological burden or chronic comorbidity.
papers.journal: Pathophysiology : the official journal of the International Society for Pathophysiology

papers.title: Citicoline as an Adjunct Therapy in Glaucoma: A Systematic Review of Clinical Outcomes and Safety.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Glaucoma is a progressive optic neuropathy characterized by retinal ganglion cell loss and visual field deterioration despite adequate intraocular pressure control. Neuroprotective adjunct therapies have therefore been investigated, and citicoline has emerged as a potential candidate. We conducted a systematic review to summarize and critically appraise the evidence on the effects of citicoline, used as an adjunctive therapy, on visual function, functional vision, and quality of life in patients with glaucoma. Methods: A systematic literature search was performed in major electronic databases (PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science) following PRISMA guidelines. Randomized and non-randomized clinical studies evaluating citicoline as adjunctive therapy in glaucoma were included. Outcomes of interest comprised visual function, electrophysiology, structural optical coherence tomography parameters, quality of life, and safety. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 and ROBINS-I tools. Results: Fifteen studies were included in this review, ten randomized controlled trials and five non-randomized clinical trials. Included studies showed heterogeneous designs and follow-up durations. Several studies reported improvements in electrophysiological responses, including retinal and post-retinal functional markers, and relative stabilization of selected visual field indices, with some studies reporting preservation of retinal nerve fiber layer and ganglion cell complex thickness under stable intraocular pressure. However, these surrogate outcomes were not consistently accompanied by improvements in visual acuity or patient-reported quality-of-life measures. Methodological limitations and endpoint variability reduced comparability across studies. Across oral, topical, and intramuscular routes of administration, citicoline was generally reported to have a favorable safety and tolerability profile. Conclusions: Current evidence suggests that citicoline may exert neurobiological effects compatible with neuroprotection in glaucoma, but the clinical significance of these findings remains uncertain. Available data are insufficient to support routine clinical recommendation. Well-designed randomized trials with standardized, patient-relevant outcomes are required to determine whether these effects translate into meaningful visual benefit.

papers.title: Association Between Caffeine Consumption and Excessive Daytime Sleepiness: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of Over 10,000 Health Science Students in Saudi Arabia.
papers.abstract: Caffeine is widely consumed by university students, but its relationship with excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) remains a concern. This study aimed to examine the associations between caffeine consumption patterns and EDS among health sciences students in Saudi Arabia. A cross-sectional study was conducted between 23 January and 18 November 2025 using a structured questionnaire and the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) to assess caffeine consumption patterns and daytime sleepiness. EDS was defined as an ESS score greater than 10. Multivariable logistic regression was used to examine associations between caffeine consumption patterns and EDS. A total of 10,074 students participated in the study, with a mean age of 22.6 ± 2.5 years; 56.0% were female. Overall, 57.6% of students experienced mild to severe EDS. Female students had higher odds of EDS than male students (aOR 2.03, 95% CI 1.87-2.21, p < 0.001). Internship students had higher odds than first-year students (aOR 1.84, 95% CI 1.53-2.20, p < 0.001), as did current smokers compared with non-smokers (aOR 1.82, 95% CI 1.60-2.06, p < 0.001). Consuming more than 400 mg of caffeine daily was associated with higher odds of EDS compared with not consuming coffee (aOR 2.10, 95% CI 1.67-2.66, p < 0.001). Evening caffeine consumption (aOR 2.26, 95% CI 1.90-2.70, p < 0.001) and coffee consumption immediately before bedtime (aOR 2.22, 95% CI 1.81-2.72, p < 0.001) were also associated with higher odds of EDS. A dose-response association was observed between daily caffeine intake and EDS, with higher intake and consumption later in the day associated with greater odds of EDS. Raising awareness of appropriate caffeine doses and timing may help promote healthier sleep habits among students.

papers.title: Circadian BMAL1/CLOCK-REV-ERB Signalling in Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's Disease and Spinal Cord Injury.
papers.abstract: BMAL1, CLOCK and nuclear receptors REV-ERBα/β are transcription factors that tie in the central nervous system between circadian timing and inflammatory and metabolic homeostasis. This is a narrative review on their functions in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and spinal cord injury, which is an acquired neuroinflammatory injury rather than a primary neurodegenerative disease. A purposive, non-systematic synthesis was undertaken based on targeted PubMed/MEDLINE searches through August 2026, and primary reports identified through the citations in the included papers. The evidence is typified by cell population, experimental manipulation and study design. Both the loss of BMAL1 and selected manipulation of microglial and astrocytic cells have been shown to increase inflammatory or neurovascular injury, while loss of BMAL1 in adult conditional deletion and pharmacological experiments suggest neutral functional outcomes, respectively, and selected manipulation of microglial and astrocytic cells suggests functional outcomes in the form of increased phagocytosis or protein clearance, respectively. Such differences make it not possible to recommend generically to activate or inhibit the clock. Putative REV-ERB ligands will need to be validated as receptor dependent and melatonin, nobiletin and dietary timing have unique and often indirect mechanisms and mostly preclinical evidence. The human studies used observation to link circadian dysruptions to neurological disease, while blood-based assays have been developed to approximate biological phase, but these studies have not provided evidence that manipulation of the clock results in better neurological outcomes. The main translational aim is to conduct testing of circadian stratification of existing treatment, and to establish the cell-specific benefits, harms and target engagement necessary to support the further development of direct clock pharmacology.

papers.title: Daytime Sleepiness and Self-Reported Sleep Characteristics Among Emergency Healthcare Workers in Public and Private Hospitals in Sana'a, Yemen.
papers.abstract: To describe daytime sleepiness and self-reported sleep characteristics among emergency healthcare workers in Sana'a, Yemen, and examine unadjusted differences between public- and private-hospital participants. This cross-sectional study included 198 physicians, nurses, and respiratory therapists selected by convenience sampling from six hospitals during February-June 2026. Responses to the eight-item Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) were summed only when all items were valid. Sleep latency, duration, and perceived sleep quality were analyzed as recorded categorical responses. Standard Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) global scores were not reconstructed because required continuous timing responses were not available. Comparisons used Welch's t test and Mann-Whitney U-tests. Complete valid ESS totals were available for 193 participants (mean 8.98 ± 4.13); 77/193 (39.9%) scored >10. Among respondents with valid item data, 143/197 (72.6%) reported <6 hours of sleep, 85/197 (43.1%) reported sleep latency >30 minutes, and 44/194 (22.7%) rated their sleep as fairly or very bad. Mean ESS scores were 9.25 ± 3.87 (public, n=101) and 8.68 ± 4.41 (private, n=92); difference 0.56 points (95% CI -0.62 to 1.75; Welch p=0.349). Hospital sector was strongly confounded with profession, shift pattern, and working hours in the available dataset. Short reported sleep duration, prolonged sleep latency, and ESS-defined excessive daytime sleepiness were common in this convenience sample. Neither comparable global PSQI results nor independent sector effects could be established. Further studies should retain standard validated questionnaire responses and strengthen the sampling design.

papers.title: The Insomnia Daytime Symptoms and Impacts Questionnaire: a qualitative interview study of content validity in insomnia disorder and comorbid conditions.
papers.abstract: The Insomnia Daytime Symptoms and Impacts Questionnaire (IDSIQ) is a 14-item patient-reported outcome (PRO) measure evaluating the effects of insomnia disorder on daytime functioning. Previous validation work for the IDSIQ did not include patients with known comorbidities such as alcohol use disorder (AUD), obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), and mild cognitive impairment due to probable Alzheimer's disease (MCI-AD), which often underlie or contribute to insomnia. We conducted cross-sectional qualitative interview studies in US adults with self-reported insomnia and comorbid AUD, OSA, or MCI-AD. Concept elicitation interviews and cognitive debriefing interviews were conducted, the latter after participants completed the IDSIQ electronically. Qualitative data were analyzed by content analysis and quantitative data through calculation of descriptive statistics. Ten participants with AUD, 20 with OSA, and 15 with MCI-AD completed interviews. Participants reported that insomnia had physical, emotional, cognitive, work-related, and social impacts and affected their ability to do daily activities. Most participants found the IDSIQ relevant to their experiences, clear, understandable, and of acceptable length. Most participants understood the response options and considered both the options and the recall period of "today" appropriate. While individual participants suggested possible changes to the IDSIQ, none of the suggestions emerged consistently such that changes to the IDSIQ seemed to be warranted. This study provides qualitative evidence supporting content validity of the IDSIQ in patients with insomnia and three comorbidities. The results indicate that the IDSIQ can be used for clinical research in patients with insomnia and three frequently associated comorbidities.

papers.title: The gut microbiome and brain inflammation in Parkinson's disease: mechanisms and therapies.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common chronic progressive neurodegenerative disorder affecting over 10 million people worldwide. PD is increasingly understood to have peripheral origins in a substantial subset of patients, in whom microbiota dysbiosis precedes and facilitates central neurodegeneration via the gut-brain axis. Dysbiosis-associated depletion of short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing bacteria, enrichment of lipopolysaccharide-producing taxa, and loss of gut barrier integrity activate toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) signaling, prime microglia towards a disease-linked phenotype, and promote the misfolding of α-synuclein and its propagation from the enteric to the central nervous system. Complement, activated by α-synuclein and shaped by the gut microbiota, further links dysbiosis to neurodegeneration. Beyond neuroinflammation, the gut microbiome modulates levodopa pharmacokinetics through bacterial tyrosine decarboxylase activity and interacts with catechol-O-methyltransferase inhibitors to alter drug bioavailability. Certain microbial metabolites, including the trimethylamine N-oxide to butyrate ratio and secondary bile acids, have emerged as candidate biomarkers. Cutaneous phosphorylated α-synuclein deposition and seeding amplification assays (SAA) are evaluated as minimally invasive peripheral biomarkers, along with epidemiological evidence linking prior antibiotic exposure and inflammatory bowel disease to PD risk. Emerging therapeutic strategies include SCFA supplementation, fecal microbiota transplantation, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonists, and targeted probiotics. Microbiome-direct strategies may benefit patients with a gut-first PD subtype, suggested by prodromal constipation, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder, or cardiac sympathetic denervation, underscoring the need for subtype-stratified trial designs. In this review article, we highlight recent evidence linking the gut microbiome with neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease through α-synuclein pathology, complement activation, and LPS/TLR4/NF-κB signaling, and discuss the implications for biomarkers, pharmacological interactions, and therapies. In conclusion, the convergence of mechanisms, biomarkers, and clinical evidence indicates the gut microbiome may be a significant diagnostic and modifiable therapeutic target in PD.

papers.title: Multi-scale feature fusion and neural architecture search for electroencephalography-based affective-state recognition in public benchmark datasets.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG)-based affective-state recognition may provide an objective neurophysiological complement to self-report scales and behavioral observations, but robust modeling remains difficult because EEG signals are non-stationary, temporally heterogeneous, and strongly subject-dependent. This study evaluated MFANet, a multi-scale feature fusion and neural architecture search-enhanced framework for binary classification of valence, arousal, and dominance. MFANet combines parallel one-dimensional convolutional branches with different receptive fields, channel-wise attention for adaptive feature recalibration, and a neural architecture search-guided long short-term memory module for temporal modeling. The framework was evaluated on the public DEAP and DREAMER datasets using five-fold, trial-grouped subject-dependent cross-validation in which all windows from one stimulus trial remained in the same outer fold and all data-dependent operations were confined to the corresponding training data. In DEAP ablation experiments, the complete model achieved mean accuracies of 97.20 ± 1.63% for valence, 97.32 ± 1.27% for arousal, and 97.14 ± 1.21% for dominance. Compared with the basic convolutional-recurrent baseline, multi-scale feature fusion and the searched recurrent module improved average accuracy by 10.17 and 10.87 percentage points, respectively, corresponding to relative gains of 12.5% and 13.4%. In participant-level paired comparisons based on the archived participant-level values, MFANet exceeded the dynamic graph convolutional neural network (DGCNN) by 4.13, 3.39, and 3.71 percentage points; bootstrap 95% confidence intervals were 3.29-5.15, 2.56-4.38, and 2.74-4.85, and all Holm-adjusted p-values were <0.001. A DEAP channel-count sensitivity analysis indicated that the full 32-channel montage changed accuracy by less than 0.4 percentage points relative to the prespecified 14-channel montage. These findings suggest that joint multi-scale representation learning and adaptive recurrent architecture selection can improve benchmark EEG affective-state recognition. Because the analysis used public healthy-volunteer datasets and self-reported affective labels, the framework should be regarded as a computational method for future clinical validation rather than a diagnostic tool.

papers.title: Correction: Responsiveness of ThymoDream® as a natural modulator of the circadian axis: a comparative RCT with melatonin supplementation employing melatonin profiling and actigraphy.
papers.abstract: [This corrects the article DOI: 10.3389/frsle.2026.1879110.].

papers.title: The potential role and value of phosphorylated tau protein in the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease: research progress.
papers.abstract: Research on the pathological mechanisms of PD has long focused on the aggregation of α-synuclein, but the role of phosphorylated tau (p-tau) protein in the onset, progression, and conversion to Parkinson's disease dementia has received increasing attention. Based on a systematic search of PubMed and Web of Science, this article reviews the physiological functions of tau protein and its neurotoxic effects after phosphorylation, and systematically summarizes the clinical and pathological evidence for p-tau at different clinical stages of PD (the prodromal stage characterized by rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder, the clinical stage dominated by motor symptoms, and the advanced stage accompanied by dementia). Crucially, we explicitly distinguish correlational human neuropathological observations from causal inference: the cascade relationship between amyloid β (Aβ) and tau pathology described in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is used only as an analogy, and the proposed "α-synuclein initiates, p-tau mediates toxicity" model for PD is presented as a hypothesis to be tested rather than as an established mechanism. By drawing on the cascade between Aβ and tau in AD, the potential timing and mechanisms of p-tau in the pathological process of PD are discussed. Furthermore, this article discusses new strategies for detecting p-tau through peripheral biomarkers such as skin biopsy to assist in the diagnosis and pathological staging of PD, while explicitly acknowledging that direct evidence for cutaneous p-tau in PD remains very limited and that current skin-biopsy data relate almost exclusively to α-synuclein; it then reviews the current status of p-tau pathology research in existing PD animal models, including the discrepancies between neurotoxin models and genuine human PD pathology, aiming to provide a theoretical basis for a comprehensive understanding of the complex pathological network of PD and the development of new therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Thyroid hormone sensitivity and cardiovascular disease in the euthyroid population: indices, mechanisms, and translational gaps.
papers.abstract: Thyroid hormones regulate cardiac contractility, electrophysiology, vascular tone, and lipid metabolism. Beyond overt thyroid disease, altered tissue sensitivity to thyroid hormone can be quantified in people with normal circulating hormone levels using central indices (TFQI, PTFQI, TSHI, TT4RI) derived from free thyroxine and TSH, and a peripheral index (the FT3/FT4 ratio). This review summarizes what these indices can and cannot tell us about cardiovascular risk. Most of the evidence is cross-sectional and comes from a small number of cohorts. Reduced sensitivity tracks most consistently with atherogenic dyslipidemia, whereas associations with arrhythmia, atherosclerosis, hypertension, and heart failure vary in direction and strength. The central indices, however, largely capture variation in the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid set point rather than tissue sensitivity, and none has been validated against a physiological reference standard. Single measurements add further uncertainty through substantial within-person variation. Two translational problems remain: the risk markers and the available TRβ-selective drugs act on different physiological axes, and almost no study has tested whether adding an index improves established risk models. Before these indices can inform clinical decisions, their repeatability and construct validity must be established, causality tested in prospective and genetic designs, and incremental predictive value demonstrated.

papers.title: Neuroinflammation in central vestibular compensation and in the pathogenesis of vestibular disorders: preclinical evidence, mechanistic bridges, and a causal research agenda.
papers.abstract: Recovery from acute vestibular damage depends on central compensation (plasticity within the vestibular nuclei) rather than on repair of the peripheral lesion. The cellular mechanisms of compensation have classically been framed in neuronal terms; over the past two decades, evidence has accumulated that glial and inflammatory processes participate in the course of compensation and can be manipulated to alter it. To map the evidence for neuroinflammation in central vestibular compensation with explicit attention to its strength, directness, and boundaries, and to derive a falsifiable mechanistic framework and research agenda. Structured PubMed search ([tiab]-restricted queries; 71 unique records screened, 69 on 2 September 2026 and 2 on a 25 October 2026 re-run; 37 included, graded A-E and by directness), supplemented by contextual pools and classic reference studies. Narrative synthesis; not a systematic review. Direct evidence is confined to 20 original preclinical studies that measured glial or inflammatory processes in vestibular models: 14 used injury or overload paradigms, in which the question is compensation, and 6 used disease models, which address pathogenesis rather than compensation. In the injury and overload paradigms, glial responses accompany deafferentation and sustained vestibular stimulation; suppressing acute inflammation (methylprednisolone), exacerbating it (LPS), or sustaining it (sleep deprivation through TLR4/NF-κB/NLRP3) all impair compensation, while interventions that alter glial abundance or marker-defined state are associated with improved recovery. In vestibular migraine and ischemic vertigo models, inflammatory pathways contribute to central sensitization. Human brain evidence identified by our structured PubMed search was limited to one TSPO-PET study in vestibular schwannoma; the search identified no direct vestibular-nucleus glial evidence in primary vestibular disorders. We propose a dual-phase, state-dependent glial hypothesis: a supportive acute window whose inflammatory level must remain "homeostatic," followed by a decompensation risk if inflammation persists or polarizes, with a separate, hypothesis-level inflammation-to-sensitization path for vestibular migraine and PPPD. Priority experiments are time-windowed cell-type-specific manipulations in models and TSPO-PET of the vestibular nuclei in acute vestibular neuritis and PPPD. Neuroinflammation is currently best regarded as a candidate modulator of vestibular compensation requiring causal validation, not an established disease mechanism.

papers.title: Impaired corneal nerve repair and regeneration after injury in mouse sleep deprivation model.
papers.abstract: To investigate the impact of sleep deprivation (SD) on corneal nerve repair and regeneration following injury and to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms. Female C57BL/6 mice, aged 10-12wk, were allocated to either the SD group or the normal control (NC) group based on sleep duration. A corneal injury model was established to evaluate the rate of corneal epithelial healing and the dynamics of wound repair. Immunofluorescence staining assessed changes in corneal basal nerve fiber density. Corneal sensitivity was measured using the Cochet-Bonnet esthesiometer. A quantitative polymerase chain reaction was conducted to determine changes in the expression of nerve growth factor (NGF) in mouse corneal tissues. Furthermore, RNA-sequencing was performed for in-depth analysis of the corneal transcriptome following epithelial injury. On day 6 post-injury, the SD group exhibited significantly lower central and peripheral corneal nerve fiber density compared with the NC group. Corneal sensitivity in the SD group was substantially lower than in the NC group. NGF expression in the cornea was significantly lower in the SD group compared with the NC group. Additionally, the corneal transcriptome of the SD group exhibited significant alterations compared to the NC group, notably a downregulation of nerve-related gene expression following SD treatment. Pathway analysis further revealed that SD inhibited multiple pathways associated with nerve repair. These findings demonstrate that SD significantly delays repair and regeneration following corneal nerve injury, providing novel theoretical perspectives into its detrimental effect on ocular health.

papers.title: A Retrospective Review of Oromyofunctional Therapy in the Treatment of Pediatric Sleep-Disordered Breathing: A Local Single-Center Study.
papers.abstract: Background and objectives Pediatric sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) ranges from primary snoring to obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Oromyofunctional therapy (OMT) aims to improve upper airway function through targeted muscle training. This study reviewed the observed clinical and polysomnography (PSG) outcomes in children with SDB receiving OMT and explored associations between treatment compliance and observed outcomes. Methods This single-center retrospective observational study reviewed medical records of children aged three to 18 years who received OMT for SDB between January 2018 and December 2024. Outcomes included caregiver-reported changes in snoring and daytime sleepiness, modified Epworth Sleepiness Scale (mESS) scores, and pre- and post-intervention PSG parameters as follows: obstructive apnea-hypopnea index (OAHI), nadir oxygen saturation (SpO2), and arousal index. A sensitivity analysis was performed in an isolated OMT subgroup, excluding patients with concurrent weight reduction, improvement in allergic rhinitis, adenotonsillectomy, or nocturnal non-invasive ventilation. Acceptable compliance was defined as completion of at least 50% of the prescribed treatment components. Results Among 48 patients (median age nine years {IQR: 7-12}; 70.8% male), snoring improved in 46/48 (95.8%) and daytime sleepiness in 26/27 (96.2%). Median mESS scores decreased from 4 (IQR: 2-7) to 1 (IQR: 0-3; p<0.001). In the isolated OMT subgroup (n=32), snoring improved in 30/32 (93.8%) and daytime sleepiness in 12/13 (92.3%); median mESS scores decreased from 4.5 (IQR: 2-7) to 1 (IQR: 0-3; p<0.001). Among the 17 patients with paired PSG data in the overall study group, median time between baseline and post-OMT PSG was 20 months (IQR: 17-27.5). COVID pandemic-induced healthcare disruptions and patient-led deferrals contributed to the extended timeline between the paired PSG evaluations. In the whole study group, median OAHI decreased from 8.7 to 2.8 events/h (p=0.015), SpO2 nadir increased from 89% to 91% (p=0.003), and median arousal index decreased from 9.6 to 6.4 events/h (p=0.006). In the isolated OMT subgroup (n=11), changes in median OAHI (8.7 to 4.9 events/h; p=0.213), SpO2 nadir (89% to 91%; p=0.050), and median arousal index (7.3 to 6.4 events/h; p=0.075) were not statistically significant. Acceptable compliance was achieved by 35/48 patients (72.9%). No significant associations were found between compliance and age, sex, or comorbidities. Significant improvement in clinical symptoms and mESS scores was observed in both compliance groups. No significant changes in PSG parameters were observed in either compliance group. Conclusion Improvement in symptoms of snoring and daytime sleepiness and reduced mESS scores were observed following OMT intervention in both the whole study group and the isolated OMT subgroup. Although PSG parameters improved significantly in the overall study group, these findings were not consistently demonstrated in the isolated OMT subgroup. Given the retrospective design, small sample size, relatively long interval between pre- and post-intervention PSGs, and potential confounding from concurrent interventions, the independent efficacy of OMT could not be established from this study. Larger prospective controlled studies are needed to evaluate the efficacy of OMT in pediatric SDB.

papers.title: Narcolepsy in the postpartum period: current evidence and future directions.
papers.abstract: Narcolepsy is a chronic sleep-wake disorder characterized by hypocretin (HCRT) deficiency, most commonly resulting from immune-mediated mechanisms targeting HCRT-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus. Although narcolepsy affects men and women at similar rates, increasing evidence suggests that female reproductive transitions influence disease expression and clinical burden. The postpartum period is characterized by abrupt endocrine changes, immune reactivation, neuroimmune remodeling, and profound behavioral adaptations, all of which intersect with biological pathways implicated in HCRT regulation. Clinical observations further suggest that this period may exacerbate pre-existing symptoms of narcolepsy and, in some cases, coincide with its first clinical manifestation. This mini review summarizes current evidence linking postpartum physiology and narcolepsy, with particular emphasis on neuroendocrine and immune mechanisms involving the HCRT system. We review clinical studies describing postpartum symptom exacerbation and postpartum-onset narcolepsy, discuss the biological plausibility of the postpartum period as a window of vulnerability, and examine the current landscape of preclinical models, highlighting the absence of experimental paradigms specifically designed to investigate pregnancy or the postpartum period. The relevance of the postpartum period extends beyond its clinical implications, offering an opportunity to investigate how reproductive physiology interacts with HCRT signaling and contributes to narcolepsy pathophysiology. This perspective may inform both the development of targeted research strategies and the clinical management of women with narcolepsy.

papers.title: Identifying Patient-Specific Factors Affecting Phantom Limb Pain to Inform Personalized Treatment.
papers.abstract: Phantom limb pain varies greatly between individuals; however, research studies typically pool data across participants. Individual person-level research may be possible by using ecological momentary assessment. The purpose of this study was to use ecological momentary assessment and causal modeling in a rehabilitation population to identify factors that affect phantom limb pain intensity on the individual participant level and to compare those to the same factors at the group level. This observational, longitudinal study included individuals (n = 17) from across the United States with lower limb amputation and phantom limb pain. Participants completed online surveys using their mobile phones three times per day for 40 days measuring pain and potentially related factors (e.g. sleep, activity, mood). Participants also reported pain episodes occurring outside of these survey times. Weather data were incorporated with survey data. Causal modeling was used to analyze relationships between pain and other factors and make predictions about factors that increase or decrease phantom limb pain intensity. Results from causal modeling showed graphs with plausible relationships that were stable during resampling analyses. Most of the factors predicted to affect phantom limb pain were unique to a single participant. Group data did not appropriately represent any individual participant datasets. These results support the idea that phantom limb pain is a personalized experience requiring individual patient-level evaluation. Personalized causal models of pain estimated from ecological momentary assessments are a promising approach for selecting evidence-based, patient-specific intervention targets.
papers.journal: Canadian journal of pain = Revue canadienne de la douleur

papers.title: Lived Experiences of Pornography Exposure among Adolescents in East Kalimantan, Indonesia: A Qualitative Study.
papers.abstract: Pornography exposure among Indonesian adolescents is a growing concern, as limited sexuality education and cultural taboos restrict open discussion of sexuality related issues. This study aimed to explore adolescents' lived experiences of pornography exposure and its psychological impacts, identify their educational needs, and examine the perspectives of key stakeholders. This qualitative study was conducted in East Kalimantan, Indonesia, between January and April 2025 following a preliminary screening survey to identify students with diverse exposure histories. Data were collected through two focus group discussions (FGDs) with adolescents and stakeholders, and six in-depth interviews (IDIs) with students. Data were analyzed thematically following Braun and Clarke's framework, with methodological triangulation applied to enhance trustworthiness. Thirteen participants were involved, consisting of six senior high school students (including two peer educators) and seven stakeholders (two school counselors, one clinical psychologist, two public health academics, one youth task force representative, and one officer from the Population and Family Planning Office). This composition of participants was selected to allow triangulation between adolescents' lived experiences and stakeholders' professional perspectives. Three overarching themes emerged: (1) ambivalent perceptions and lived experiences of pornography, (2) psychological, academic, and social consequences, including intrusive thoughts, sleep disturbance, declining performance, aggression, and imitative risk taking; (3) educational needs and preferences. Adolescents reported curiosity, guilt, secrecy, intrusive thoughts, sleep difficulties, and reduced concentration. They preferred short digital videos and supportive peer led discussions over conventional seminars. Stakeholders emphasized stronger school family collaboration. Adolescents described pornography exposure as intertwined with curiosity, guilt, and secrecy, alongside perceived difficulties in daily life. Findings support the development of culturally sensitive, peer led digital education with school and family involvement.

papers.title: Acute Encephalopathy in a Patient with Dravet Syndrome Successfully Managed with Therapeutic Normothermia and Vitamin Supplementation Therapy: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Acute encephalopathy associated with Dravet syndrome (DS-AE) is a life-threatening complication associated with poor neurological outcomes. However, treatment strategies for this condition have yet to be established. Herein, we report the case of a patient with DS-AE who showed substantial neurological recovery following multidisciplinary treatment involving targeted temperature management (TTM) and vitamin supplementation, indicating the potential utility of this therapeutic approach. A 3-year-4-month-old girl with clinically diagnosed Dravet syndrome developed febrile convulsive status epilepticus associated with respiratory syncytial virus infection. Although seizures were terminated by treatment with intravenous midazolam, the patient remained comatose, and the electroencephalography demonstrated diffuse slow-wave activity, leading to a diagnosis of DS-AE. She was treated with intensive care, including continuous midazolam infusion; TTM for 48 hours; and vitamin supplementation with thiamine, pyridoxine, and L-carnitine. Despite diffuse cerebral atrophy on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in the acute phase, she gradually recovered and within 4 months of the onset returned to the developmental status achieved before DS-AE onset, with subsequent improvement in cerebral atrophy on follow-up MRI. Multidisciplinary treatment, including TTM and vitamin supplementation, may represent a therapeutic strategy to reduce neurological sequelae in patients with DS-AE.

papers.title: Students' and teachers' perceptions of a gamified app-based well-being intervention (GABWI) in Finland and Estonia.
papers.abstract: Recent research has highlighted concerns about adolescents' physical activity, sleep patterns, and eating habits, while also suggesting that digital platforms could support adolescents' holistic well-being. The study examines how students and teachers perceive a gamified, app-based well-being intervention (GABWI) and its potential effects on students' views of their holistic well-being and physical capacity after Move! measurements. Move! is a national system in Finland that monitors and provides feedback on students' physical capacity. The study used the Intervention Mapping model and a mixed-methods design. The eight-week GABWI was implemented in Finland and Estonia and included 94 students aged 13-16 years and seven teachers. Data included student health questionnaires and interviews with students (n = 24) and teachers (n = 7). The quantitative data were analysed using exploratory factor analysis and t-tests, and the interview data using content analysis. The findings suggest that GABWI may influence adolescents' perceptions of their holistic well-being and physical capacity. Students perceived that using the app for Move! measurements was more motivating than traditional teacher-led methods. GABWI offers new opportunities to support students' holistic well-being and may facilitate data-driven decision-making and resource allocation to specific areas or student groups.

papers.title: Cardiac autonomic and behavioral signatures of clinically meaningful weight loss: a 12-week wearable study of 31,126 adults.
papers.abstract: Achieving ≥5% body weight loss is clinically meaningful for reducing cardiometabolic risk, yet most evidence on the physiological and behavioral correlates of early weight loss comes from small, supervised interventions. Whether these adaptations replicate using consumer wearable data in free-living adults is unclear. We analyzed 12 weeks of near-continuous wearable data from 31,126 adults (37.4 ± 10.4 years, 79% male, BMI 29.7 ± 4.2 kg/m2) who initiated a weight-loss goal within a consumer health platform (WHOOP). Participants achieving ≥5% weight loss (n = 4,465; 14.3%) were 1:1 propensity-matched to participants who did not (3,912 pairs; N = 7,824). We compared trajectories of cardiac autonomic function (heart rate variability [HRV], resting heart rate [RHR]), physical activity (Strain), sleep, application engagement, and artificial intelligence (AI) Coach interactions. The weight loss group lost 7.5% of body weight versus 0.9% in the matched group, with greater improvements in HRV (+2.78 ms, 95% CI [1.71, 3.85]) and RHR (-1.75 bpm [-2.10, -1.40]) by Week 12, with between-group differences emerging at Week 4. Physical activity was the strongest behavioral predictor of clinically meaningful weight loss (β = -0.72 [-0.77, -0.67]; OR = 1.22 per Strain unit, 95% CI [1.19, 1.24]). Application engagement and AI Coach interactions, particularly motivation and exercise discussions, were independently associated with ≥5% weight loss and percent weight change. Consumer wearables can capture physiological and behavioral signatures of clinically meaningful early weight loss in free-living adults.

papers.title: Clinical Severity, Resuscitation Characteristics, and Early Outcomes of Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy Among Newborns at Banadir Hospital, Mogadishu, Somalia.
papers.abstract: Detailed neonatal encephalopathy data from Somalia are limited. We described recorded severity, resuscitation characteristics, and outcomes among newborns classified as having hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) at Banadir Hospital. This exploratory post hoc secondary analysis included 26 newborns with recorded HIE from a parent analytical cross-sectional study of 315 live-born newborns at Banadir Hospital, conducted from 11 January to 20 March 2026. Thompson totals recorded at 5 minutes defined mild (1-10), moderate (11-14) and severe (15-22) categories. All infants received bag-mask positive-pressure ventilation (PPV). Duration ran from PPV initiation until one of three events: recovery without further PPV; intubation; or death. Outcomes were assessed within 24 hours. Analyses were descriptive and unadjusted. Thompson categories comprised 14 mild, six moderate and six severe cases. Median PPV-episode duration was 20.0, 22.5 and 35.0 minutes across increasing categories (Kruskal-Wallis p=0.003). Five deaths occurred within 24 hours: one, zero and four, respectively. Seizures were clinically diagnosed in 25 newborns without electroencephalographic (EEG) confirmation, including 13 in the mild score category; one seizure flag was undocumented. Intubation and resuscitation-medication data were not collected. In this small selected subgroup, higher Thompson categories accompanied longer recorded PPV episodes and more deaths within 24 hours. Findings are hypothesis-generating. Clinical seizure ascertainment, limited assessment documentation and the short observation window limit interpretation. Long-term outcomes were not assessed.

papers.title: Structural and functional characterization of the KCNJ6 G154C variant reveals severe GIRK2 channel gain-of-function and opportunities for drug repurposing.
papers.abstract: G protein-gated inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK2) channels regulate neuronal excitability and are implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders. A rare KCNJ6 variant, G154C (hGIRK2G154C), was identified in a patient with mild Keppen-Lubinsky syndrome features, contrasting with severe phenotypes linked to other selectivity-filter mutations. Here we combined molecular dynamics simulations and patch-clamp electrophysiology to characterize the hGIRK2G154C mutant, revealing a widened selectivity filter that resulted in loss of potassium selectivity, aberrant sodium permeation, and loss of inward rectification, indicating a severe gain-of-function phenotype. An in silico and electrophysiological drug screen identified FDA-approved compounds, including nefazodone and eletriptan, that potently inhibited hGIRK2 and hGIRK2G154C through distinct blocking mechanisms. These findings elucidate the structural and functional impact of the G154C mutation and identify potent pharmacological tools and starting points for therapeutic development in hGIRK2 channelopathies.

papers.title: Task exposure and stimulation duration modulate HD-tDCS effects on working memory in older adults.
papers.abstract: Age-related working-memory decline has been associated with altered neural oscillations, and high-definition transcranial direct current stimulation (HD-tDCS) may improve cognition. However, responses vary and may depend on prior task engagement and stimulation duration. We examined these factors in a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled crossover study of 39 healthy older adults (65.4 ± 3.0 years). Participants received real and sham 2-mA HD-tDCS over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex for 10 or 20 min. Task exposure before real stimulation was determined by stimulation sequence, creating less- and more-exposure groups. Working-memory performance and EEG spectral power were assessed during two-back tasks before and after stimulation. Change in discrimination sensitivity (Δd') showed a Stimulation × Duration × Exposure interaction. Exploratory comparisons indicated that 10-min real stimulation improved Δd' relative to sham in the less-exposure group but reduced Δd' in the more-exposure group; neither 20-min subgroup showed a significant effect. Secondary inverse-efficiency analyses showed improved efficiency after real stimulation under less exposure and poorer efficiency under more exposure. The more-exposure, 10-min group also showed increased central beta power following real stimulation. Associations between beta-power changes and poorer behavioral performance did not remain significant after false-discovery-rate correction. These findings suggest that HD-tDCS effects vary with stimulation duration and prior task context. However, the small subgroups and confounding of task exposure with stimulation order and session position require cautious interpretation. Larger studies independently manipulating exposure and stimulation order are needed to confirm these potentially state-dependent effects.

papers.title: Maladaptive state allocation: an orexin-based framework linking sleep disturbance, chronic pain, and substance use disorder.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbance, chronic pain, and substance use disorders are highly prevalent conditions that frequently co-occur and exacerbate one another. Although traditionally studied as distinct clinical entities, growing evidence suggests they share common neurobiological mechanisms. Among these, the orexin (OX; also known as hypocretin) system has emerged as a critical regulator of arousal, motivation, stress responsiveness, and nociception, positioning it as a potential contributor to interactions among sleep, pain, and addiction. In this review, we propose that OX may function as a state-integration network that coordinates behavioral responses to competing physiological and environmental demands. Through widespread projections to brainstem, thalamic, limbic, and mesolimbic circuits, OX transmission dynamically regulates vigilance, salience attribution, pain modulation, and reward-seeking behavior. Under physiological conditions, these actions promote adaptive behavioral prioritization. However, chronic dysregulation of OX transmission may result in maladaptive state allocation characterized by persistent hyperarousal, amplified pain-related salience, and excessive motivational value assigned to drug-associated cues. We synthesize experimental evidence implicating OX-dependent circuits in the pathophysiology of sleep disturbance, chronic pain, and substance use disorder and introduce a conceptual triad model linking these conditions. Within this framework, we propose that sleep loss may increase pain sensitivity and craving, chronic pain may disrupt sleep and promote substance use, and repeated drug exposure may further destabilize sleep and pain regulation, creating a self-reinforcing cycle. Finally, we discuss individual factors that may influence vulnerability to triadic comorbidity and highlight emerging therapeutic approaches targeting the OX system.

papers.title: Development and Useability of a Lifestyle Program Designed to Address Depressive Symptoms in In-Home Aged Care Recipients.
papers.abstract: Depressive symptoms are experienced by a significant proportion of older adults who receive in-home aged care services. A lifestyle program delivered through guided self-help was developed to help manage mild depressive symptoms. This study describes the development of the program and evaluates its useability. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with in-home aged care recipients across two phases. Phase 1 (N = 29) determined the content of the lifestyle program. Thematic analysis informed by grounded theory, indicated participants' support for content focused on physical activity, social connections, diet, sleep, relaxation, mindfulness meditation, and depression psychoeducation. Phase 2 (N = 28) analysed users' views about the lifestyle program. Content analysis of interviews determined that most participants found the program user-friendly. Feedback indicated a need for greater clinician involvement, reduced volume of information, and development of a protocol to tailor the program to individual needs and preferences. A tailored lifestyle program has the potential to address the emotional well-being of in-home aged care recipients.

papers.title: Shared sleep fragmentation in undergraduate roommates: dyadic actigraphy in a dense urban campus setting.
papers.abstract: Dyadic sleep research has focused on romantic partners, leaving open whether nonromantic people who share a sleep space show related sleep. We examined sleep continuity and roommate concordance among undergraduate roommate dyads on a dense urban campus bordered by an interstate highway, freight-rail corridors, and an overnight air-cargo hub. The setting is described as context; no environmental exposure was measured. Baseline data were analyzed from 29 roommate dyads (58 participants aged 18-19 years) enrolling in a mindfulness program at the University of Louisville in 2017. Participants were instructed to wear wrist actigraphs for four nights and completed one-week versions of the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and Perceived Stress Scale. The planned analysis estimated roommate concordance with intraclass correlations (ICC); analyses of same-night covariation, bedroom sharing, and perceived stress were exploratory. To separate roommate similarity from shared calendar timing, roommates were compared with same-wave non-roommates (pseudo-dyads), and night-level analyses were adjusted for day of week and week of semester. Participants averaged 6.98 h of sleep, 66 min of wake after sleep onset (WASO), and 18.6 actigraphy-detected awakenings per night. Roommate concordance was clearest for awakening frequency (ICC = 0.38, 95% CI [0.04, 0.68]), which exceeded pseudo-dyad concordance (mean ICC = 0.09); after centering on data-collection wave it was lower and imprecise (ICC = 0.25 [-0.11, 0.59]). Six other actigraphy outcomes had smaller estimates, with intervals including zero. Roommates' night-to-night deviations in WASO were correlated (r = 0.29 [0.07, 0.44]); this association persisted after day-of-week and week-of-semester adjustment and exceeded 95% of pseudo-dyad re-pairings, whereas same-night covariation in awakenings did not. Bedroom-sharing comparisons (18 vs. 10 dyads) were too imprecise to be informative. Perceived stress was associated with participants' own PSQI scores (β = 0.55 [0.39, 0.71]) and, more weakly, their own WASO (β = 0.23 [0.04, 0.43]). Undergraduate roommates showed modest similarity in sleep fragmentation that was not fully explained by shared calendar timing, extending dyadic sleep research beyond romantic partners. Because environmental exposures were not measured, the findings cannot be attributed to the urban setting; studies pairing dyadic sleep measurement with synchronized environmental monitoring are needed.

papers.title: English immersive game participation and attention, emotional health, and cognitive function in children: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Screen exposure is an important issue for children's health. The existing research pays more attention to the duration of use, but not to the content type and immersion experience. English immersion game integrates language learning and game mechanism, which belongs to educational digital behavior. This study analyzes the daily English game duration, immersion and English integration of children aged 6-14, and their relationships with attention, working memory, executive function and emotional behavior. This retrospective cross-sectional study included 215 children. Based on the parents' questionnaire, the data of English game participation were obtained: daily duration, 1-5 immersion self-evaluation, and English integration. The outcome includes all kinds of attention, working memory, executive function, emotion and ADHD symptoms. Multivariate linear regression controls total screen time, sleep, physical activity, age, gender and family SES. CPT, Flanker and Corsi were the main outcomes, and after Bonferroni correction, the four executive function and behavior indicators were set as exploratory outcomes, which were not corrected. English game time is positively correlated with selective attention (β = 0.218, p = 0.001). It is significantly different from the primary analysis of working memory, and its effect size fell below the minimum-detectable-effect threshold following Bonferroni correction. Immersion self-rating is positively correlated with multiple attention and working memory, and negatively correlated with emotional symptoms. The degree of English integration is positively correlated with cognitive indicators and negatively correlated with emotional symptoms; After excluding the pure-English-immersion subgroup, the association with selective attention and inhibition control is no longer significant, and it is regarded as descriptive association. Daily screen time was negatively correlated with cognitive ability, and positively correlated with mood and ADHD symptoms (all p < 0.001). Different dimensions of English immersion games are related to children's cognitive and emotional outcomes. In addition to the duration of use, the integration of game English is as important as the immersion experience. The results can provide reference for family digital activity selection, children's screen behavior norms and campus digital education intervention, which still needs to be verified by longitudinal research.

papers.title: Factors associated with fatigue in systemic lupus erythematosus: a cross-sectional structural equation modeling analysis of depressive symptoms as a potential mediator.
papers.abstract: This study examined physiological, psychological, and environmental factors associated with fatigue in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and assessed whether depressive symptoms statistically mediated the relationships between these factors and fatigue. A convenience sample of 252 patients with SLE was recruited from the Department of Rheumatology and Immunology, Second Hospital of Hebei Medical University, between June 2023 and June 2024. Guided by the Theory of Unpleasant Symptoms (TOUS), candidate variables were classified into physiological (including disease activity on the SLEDAI-2K, anemia, biologic agent use, and sleep disturbance), psychological (anxiety and depressive symptoms), and environmental factors (including employment status and social support). Pain severity and other clinically recorded variables were entered as covariates. Validated measures included the Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS), Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS), Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), and Social Support Rating Scale (SSRS). Univariate analyses, Spearman correlation analysis, and multivariable linear regression were performed using SPSS 26.0. Structural equation modeling (SEM) and indirect-effect testing based on bootstrapping (2,000 resamples; percentile 95% confidence intervals) were performed in R (lavaan). Sensitivity analyses (robust estimation, a Bollen-Stine bootstrap, and covariate-adjusted and alternative mediator models) were also performed. Social support, depressive symptoms, sleep disturbance, pain severity, biologic agent use, and employment status were found to be independently related to fatigue. Moreover, social support and sleep disturbance each had a significant indirect relationship with fatigue via depressive symptoms. The indirect associations persisted after clinical covariates were specified as predictors of both depressive symptoms and fatigue. However, social support was not independently associated with the binary fatigue outcome (FSS ≥ 4; OR = 0.96 per SD, P = 0.837). In this cross-sectional sample, social support, depressive symptoms, sleep disturbance, pain severity, biologic agent use, and employment status were associated with fatigue, and depressive symptoms showed a statistically significant indirect association with fatigue through pathways linking social support and sleep disturbance. Because the data are cross-sectional, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory indirect associations that are compatible with, but do not establish, a mediating mechanism, and as hypothesis-generating rather than evidence of causality or treatment effect. Systematic assessment of social support and depressive symptoms, together with dynamic evaluation of sleep disturbance and pain, may inform comprehensive fatigue assessment, while longitudinal and interventional studies are needed before firm clinical recommendations can be made.

papers.title: Drug-resistant infantile spasms with focal onset in encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis harboring a somatic mosaic KRAS mutation: a case report and literature review.
papers.abstract: Encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis (ECCL) is a rare neurocutaneous syndrome. The diagnostic detection rate of somatic mosaic KRAS mutations in ECCL has increased with the implementation of high-depth tissue next-generation sequencing (NGS).
